title: Introduction to Flight
about: This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering. a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion. b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures, propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions. c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems. d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering. a. Explain the principles of flight by describing the four fundamental forces (lift, weight, thrust, and drag) and their interactions during flight. b. Analyse atmospheric effects on flight by interpreting how atmospheric properties influence aircraft performance and operations. c. Apply basic aerodynamic concepts to evaluate the performance of airfoil, wings, and aircraft under various flight conditions. Page 1 of 5 Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC - UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION d. Evaluate aircraft performance by estimating take-off, climb, cruise, descent, landing, range, and endurance characteristics using fundamental engineering principles. e. Describe aircraft stability and control and explain how control surfaces affect aircraft motion and manoeuvrability. f. Compare aircraft propulsion systems, including propellerand jet-powered engines, and explain their operating principles and performance characteristics. g. Learn Hypersonic flight, concepts of Newtonian theory and its application to Hypersonic vehicles. h. Solve introductory flight-related engineering problems using mathematics, physics, and computational tools where appropriate. Interpret the relationship between aircraft design and flight performance, recognizing how design choices affect efficiency, safety, and operational capability. j. Communicate technical concepts related to flight through written reports, calculations, and engineering discussions

about: Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant tissues and Cell cycle analysis. The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. title: CELL BIOLOGY

The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure, intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms and related experimental procedures. title: INTEGRATED BIOLOGY
about: The course intends to bridge the gap and open new vistas to students taking up biology. The course covers two tracks, essentially. The first track introduces the student to the ordering that helps biologists to actually study the vast diversity of the living world. This track would encompass questions related to the origin and evolutionary pathways followed in nature, as well as the methods followed by biologists to systematically categorize and document them. The second track highlights the uses and applications of biology in everyday life – whether in the economic or in the social realms. Together, the course projects the subject in a way from which the student can choose and implement his biological knowledge vis-à-vis his/her interests. Being the second course on General Biology, the course exposes the students to the foundational aspects as described above. At the end of the course, the student will have developed a basic understanding of the evolutionary processes, rationale for taxonomic arrangements and familiarity of selected, representative members of the major kingdoms of living organisms. Further, the student will also become aware of how knowledge of biology (both botany and zoology) is applied for benefit of mankind and other organisms. a. To understand the scientific basis of evolution in populations b. To apply the evolutionary knowledge in classification scheme of organisms

title: RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY
about: The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems and whole genome approaches will be covered. Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology. title: Animal Physiology
about: Basic functional processes in animals; like homeostasis, membrane physiology, digestive, respiratory, excretory, circulatory, reproductive, nervous, sensory, muscular, endocrine systems will be studied at structural, functional, cellular and molecular level. This course attempts to bring the awareness among students for major features of animal physiology and corelate that to the human physiology. Emphasis will be on structure and function relationship and importanc of every organ. In addition, the course will also discuss about some of the diseases that are associated with complication in different organs. a. Integration of multiple organ systems to regulate and maintain homeostasis between the internal and external environments. b. Explore the process of enzymatic digestion and its physiological outcomes within the digestive tract. c. Functional mechanisms of the human kidneys in regulating fluid homeostasis and urine formation. d. Overview of the cardiac cycle, electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, types of circulatory vessels, regulation of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the various cellular components of blood. e. Anatomical and functional organization of nervous system, including its structural and spatial characteristics. f. The role of hormones in regulating homeostasis and supporting essential physiological functions. g. Understanding gas partial pressures, intrapleural pressure dynamics, lung volumes and capacities, respiratory disorders, and the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin. h. Study of sarcomere structure, the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction, the physiological basis of rigor mortis, and the phenomenon of muscle twitching. Exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing gametogenesis, fertilization, and progression of pregnancy.

title: Biomolecular Modeling
about: Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding, Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice models, usage of modeling packages. The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and structural biology. It describes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data in a research or industry laboratory environment.

title: ENZYMOLOGY
about: Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins. This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students.
topics: L#1-2: Broad overview of the subject and field of Enzymology and Quick preview of the entire course contents.
L# 3-4: Brief history of Enzymology; EC system of classification; Main classes of enzymes, with examples.
III Enzyme structure, conformations, and specificity of enzyme actions
L# 5-7: Enzyme structure and conformations; Types of enzyme specificity; Specificity Hypotheses.
IV Enzyme Kinetics & Mechanism of enzyme action and regulation

L# 8-11: Introduction to catalysis and kinetics; Kinetics of single-substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions; Enzyme inhibition; Kinetics of multi- substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Mechanisms of catalysis with examples; Enzymes and metabolic regulation; Investigation of active site structure.
L# 12-19: Extraction of enzymes; Enzyme assay methods; Enzyme purification techniques.
VI Instrumental techniques in enzymatic analysis
L# 20-21: Various Instrumental techniques used in Enzymatic analysis
L# 24-26: Methods of immobilization, Properties of immobilized enzymes and Applications

L# 27-35: Applications of enzymes and enzymatic analysis in clinical medicine, biotechnology, and pharmacology; Industrial Production of enzymes and applications (examples: in Food, Process industry).
X Recent advances and Innovations in Enzyme Technology

L# 36-38: Enzyme & Co-factor engineering – Current trends and Future prospects in Pharmaceutical & Fermentation Industries. Enzymes & Biosensors; Latest advances in enzymes - Industrial and Research-applications will be discussed.
L# 39: Pointers for R&D and industrial applications of enzymes

title: ENVIRONMENTAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND WASTE
about: Application of biotechnology to the management of environmental problems. Biotechnology for enhanced plant and animal production through biological insecticides, herbicides resistance, mineral cycling, conservation of genetic resources and biological nitrogen fixation. Use of biotechnological processes for pollution control, bioremediation of toxicants and treatment of domestic and industrial wastes. Ethical issues related with the release of genetically modified organism. The major objective of this course is to impart knowledge on application of biotechnological processes for betterment of environment. This course is designed to make the student understand the various biological phenomena, which can be exploited to save environment from eventual deterioration.

title: BIOSTATISTICS & BIOMODELING
about: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations. The student would learn how to collect data suitable for statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of significance.

title: Advanced Cell and Molecular Biology
about: The course deals with in-depth aspects of molecular biology of eukaryotic cell. We will discuss about molecules regulating and functional in Eukaryotic cell cycle: restriction point, G1 phase progression, role of cyclin and CKIs, cell cycle & cancer, metastasis, molecular chaperones, apoptosis and necrosis, Extra cellular matrix & adhesion, growth factors, cell signal transduction, stem cells and their potential in therapy, transport in and out of nucleus. This course will give insights to the students into some frontier areas in cell and molecular biology helping students understand the overall functioning of a cell under different environmental conditions including presence or absence of mitogens/ nutrition/ stress conditions, etc.. This will enable student draw concept map about different cell functions and related proteins. Molecular Biology of the Cell (7th/ 6th edition), Bruce Alberts, Alexander Johnson, Julian Lewis, David Morgan, Martin Raff, Keith Roberts and Peter Walter. Garland Publishing Inc., New York and London, 2022. R1. Molecular Cell Biology (Ninth Edition), Lodish, Berk, Krieger, Scott, Bretscher, Ploegh, Matsudaira. Freeman, 2022.
topics: Course Orientation, discussion on mode of conductance of various evaluation components, seminar topics, etc
Cell cycle Overview, different phases, cell cycle control and regulatory components, control of cell division and cell growth, Cyclin Kinase inhibitors
Mechanism of cell death with special reference to apoptosis and necrosis, cascade of apoptosis implications
Mechanism of protein folding in E.coli and mammalian systems, Molecular chaperones, Protein trafficking across cell and export, Proteolysis

Mechanisms of signal transduction by cell surface receptor proteins (G proteins, enzyme coupled receptors), growth factors and their interaction with receptors in cell proliferation and its regulation, JAK – STAT, Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, NF- B pathways.
Molecular basis of cancer, Cancer as micro-evolutionary process, cancer critical genes, molecular basis of cancer – cell behavior.
Mechanism for the transport of RNA and “Cargo” proteins into and out of nucleus

title: ENZYMOLOGY
about: Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins. This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students.

title: Food Biotechnology
about: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed. The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

title: Social Conduct 1
about: Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity & Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety. This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior and building awareness against substance abuse. At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community.

title: Science, Technology and Modernity
about: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.
topics: Fundamentals of technology and scientific knowledge systems
The Kuhnian revolution; Industrial Revolution; The Social Construction of Scientific and Technical Realities; Actor- Network Theory
Knowledge protection; Innovation process; Spatial dimensions of innovation; Technology diffusion; Policy debates in innovation
Stratification and Discrimination; Political economy of technology transfer; Role of power; Just Transition

title: General Mathematics III
about: Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method, Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming (Unconstrained optimization). The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of the most important practical concepts in mathematics. Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various fields of study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing. Apply the concepts of matrix algebra, systems of linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, and eigenvalues/eigenvectors to solve mathematical problems arising in science and engineering. Formulate and solve linear programming problems using graphical and simplex-based methods, analyze duality and post-optimality, and apply optimization techniques to transportation and assignment problems. Analyze and solve basic nonlinear optimization problems using appropriate numerical optimization techniques, and interpret the results in the context of engineering and pharmaceutical applications.

title: Environmental Studies
about: Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment. The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (florafauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas.

title: Introduction to Engineering Design
about: This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and management of larger open-ended, team-based engineering design tasks in a project-based learning environment. Students will learn to create detailed designs of real-world products and systems by applying design thinking and scientific principles. Students will learn a range of design techniques to contextualize, evaluate, and communicate designs, from generating ideas via sketching to development of digital models and detailed technical drawings that meet the international standards. Students will develop foundation skills in computer-aided design (CAD) techniques to generate 3D models of products and assemblies and learn to integrate them in augmented and virtual reality tools. Course Contents: Engineering Design process, Introduction to Engineering Drawing, Introduction to Orthographic Projections, Projections of points, lines, planes, and solid objects, Sectional views, Manufacturing processes and materials, Fits and Tolerances, Isometric Drawing, Introduction to Solid Modelling, Assembly drawings Apply key elements of the design process and scientific principles to create detailed design of a product that meets engineering requirements and standards. Generate and interpret engineering technical drawings of parts and assemblies according to engineering design standards; and Use CAD software to generate a computer model of a well-defined part or assembly.

title: GAME THEORY & ITS APPLICATIONS
about: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finiteand infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems. Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting. The course would aim to illustrate economic & other real-world concepts and to make students adept at approaching financial problems from a game-theoretic perspective. ) Understand the Fundamentals of Game Theory, including game construction, analysis, and solutions. ) Able to apply game theory tools to real-world contexts such as economic, political & environmental settings, trade negotiations, environmental agreements, cartels, oligopolistic competition, and in social choice contexts, among others. ) Understand the collective decision-making mechanisms using game-theoretic tools. ) Gain exposure to games with imperfect Information, including understanding the basic concepts of Bayesian games (types, beliefs, and strategies). ) Develop problem-solving and strategic thinking skills.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Robotics
about: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics. This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. title: FUZZY LOGIC & APPLICATIONS
about: Fuzzy sets, fuzzy binary relations, fuzzy logic, fuzzy reasoning, applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence etc. The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts of fuzzy sets, fuzzy relations, fuzzy logic, and fuzzy reasoning, along with their applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical, computational, and problem-solving skills through real-world applications. Each student is required to undertake a project involving the application of fuzzy logic, which may be study-oriented, computer-oriented, simulation-based, or model-based, and provides an opportunity to explore research articles and recent developments in fuzzy logic and its applications. Explain the fundamental concepts and mathematical foundations of fuzzy sets, fuzzy numbers, fuzzy relations, and fuzzy logic. Formulate and analyze problems involving fuzzy relations, fuzzy reasoning, fuzzy inference, and related logical structures. Apply fuzzy logic techniques to real-world problems in decision making, control systems, expert systems, artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Develop and evaluate a fuzzy logic-based project using appropriate computational tools, with reference to relevant research literature and contemporary applications.
topics: Basic concepts, set operations, properties, and representation of crisp sets.
Introduction to fuzzy sets, membership functions, representations, operations, and basic properties.
Advanced concepts of fuzzy sets, α- cuts, support, core, height, normality, convexity, and related properties.
Definition, types, representation, arithmetic operations, and applications of fuzzy numbers.
Fuzzy binary relations, representation, properties, composition, and related operations.
Propositions, logical connectives, truth tables, predicates, quantifiers, and logical structures.
Fuzzy propositions, linguistic variables, fuzzy connectives, implications, and basic fuzzy logic concepts.
Fuzzy rules, inference mechanisms, fuzzy reasoning, and rule-based systems.
Boolean variables, Boolean functions, switching functions, Boolean operations, and fundamental laws.
Fuzzy decision making, control systems, expert systems, and artificial intelligence.
Application-oriented modeling and analysis of fuzzy systems.
Basic concepts, formulation, interpretation, and applications of fuzzy probability.
Basic concepts, artificial neurons, network structures, and learning principles.
Integration of fuzzy logic concepts through applications, computational exercises, and project-oriented work.

title: Introduction to Nano Science
about: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered. The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.
topics: Course introduction, what is nanoscience and nanotechnology? Difference between micro and nano, classification of nanostructured materials, unique properties of nanomaterials: structural, electronic, magnetic, optical, mechanical.
Bottom-up: physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), sol- gel, spray conversion, wet chemical synthesis, self- assembly
Top-Down: Mechanical alloying, equal channel angular pressing, high-pressure torsion (HPT), accumulative roll bonding (ARB), Nanolithography
Basics of quantum physics, wave mechanics, Schrödinger wave equation, concepts of quantum well, wire and dots, tunneling, applications of quantum mechanics in nanotechnology.
Synthesis, properties, and applications of carbon nanostructures: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, nanodiamonds, and diamond-like carbon (DLC).
Applications of nanotechnology in electronics: Basics of semiconductor devices, MOSFETs, FinFETs
Application of nanotechnology in medical devices: Basics of bio- electronic devices, nanosensors, molecular imaging, targeted drug delivery applications.
Application of nanotechnology in MEMS: Basics of MEMS/NEMS, fabrication techniques, working principles of accelerometers, and actuators.
Basics of fuel cells and batteries, nanotechnology applications in fuel cells, energy storage devices.
Basics of catalysis, synthesis of metal and oxide active phases, nanoreactors.
Nanofluids Synthesis, characterization and applications relevant to heat transfer. State of the art and future research directions.
Large scale manufacture and technological issues

title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment
about: This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macroand nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology. Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3 modules as decribed below. o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout). o Introduce the importance and application of nanomaterials and the origin of their unique properties. o Summarize the fabrication methods, characterization techniques, and operating principles of solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and CNT-based energy storage systems. o Explain the merits and motivation in the renewable energy and environmental sectors. o Define toxic effect of nanomaterials on human and environment, relative remediation and precautions. title: Pattern Recognition
about: This is a first course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation and description and finally the object recognition. During the course, a flavour of matlab programming will also be given. Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to verification of signatures, and from analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of fingerprints and human blood cells. Currently, pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, necessary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.

title: Cryptography
about: This course is an introduction to the basic theory and practice of cryptographic techniques used in information security. The course is intended to understand the mathematical concepts used for designing cryptosystems. The focus would be on the mathematical concepts from Number Theory and Abstract Algebra. We will delve into topics such as encryption (private-key and public-key), digital signatures, user authentication, key management, cryptographic hashing, Network security protocols, public-key infrastructure, digital rights management, and advancement in modern cryptology such as Identity Based Encryption, Steganography and Watermarking, Post-Quantum Cryptography, and ZeroKnowledge protocols. Prerequisites: The course is self-contained, however a basic understanding of probability theory, complexity theory, and modular arithmetic from number theory would be helpful. The course is intended for advanced undergraduates and master students. Lectures deal with mathematical cryptography and related mathematical concepts required for modern cryptography and information security. The objective is to discuss and learn about basic tools and applications used in modern cryptography and to learn about some cryptographic protocols. On successful completion of the course students should be able to: understand basic principles and results of the theory of secure communication; know principles and problems of basic cryptosystems for encryption (both private and public key), digital signing and authentication; know methods to create core cryptographic protocols primitives; analyze and practically use simple cryptosystems; be understand basic principles of post-quantum cryptography and steganography. _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division Course Learning Outcomes. Design and Analyse common cryptanalytic attacks and tools. Design secure communication mechanisms for the real-world using appropriate cryptographic primitives. title: New Venture Creation
about: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guestlectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business. NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?

title: Introduction to Large Language Models
about: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs); prompt engineering techniques (e.g., zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), autonomous prompt optimization; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector databases, multi-modal RAG methods; tool and function calling; multi-agent workflows (memory, planning, action, reflection); safety, guardrails, reliability; LLM-based evaluation, human evaluation; life cycle of LLM training, LLM architecture, fine-tuning LLMs using supervised learning or reinforcement learning; inference optimization; Mechanistic Interpretability; real-world case-studies a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs. b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge bases. c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models. d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs. e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks. f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments. g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning. h. Evaluate the performance and accuracy of LLM-powered applications using appropriate metrics. Understand the principles of inference for deploying LLM models efficiently at scale.

title: Creating and Leading Entrepreneurial Organization
about: Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship; Elements of Leadership; Identifying Business Opportunities; Market Study and Research; Business Plans; Finance, Issues in Raising Finance, Venture Capitalist Evaluation of Business Plans, Technical Aspects for the Project; Corporate Strategies for Growth; Legal Aspects to entrepreneurship; People Skills; Marketing and Branding; Creativity and Communication. This Course is about creating, managing, and leading an organization. This course helps in creating an entrepreneurial mindset, developing entrepreneurial skills and equipping students with the basic knowledge necessary for an entrepreneur. The course shall enable the participants to acquire and equip themselves with requisite knowledge and skills to start and run a business successfully, which is divided into personal skills (entrepreneurial skills) and those to start a company (Start-up tools). a. To understand about entrepreneurship and getting inspiration from successful entrepreneurs. b. To learn about idea generation, opportunity assessment and evaluation and the process to create, build, and lead an entrepreneurial organization. c. To learn about nitty gritty of preparation of Business Plan. d. To know about different sources of funding and identify an appropriate source of funding for the venture. e. To learn about launching a business venture and growing it to next level of growth. 1
topics: Understanding and appreciating the importance of Entrepreneurship: The roller coaster ride of entrepreneurship, Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship, Entrepreneurship vs Intrapreneurship, Risks, Challenges, Uncertainty

Entrepreneurial Leadership: Leader vs Manager, Principled Centered Leadership, Entrepreneurial Leadership, Case studies on some of the most successful business Leaders. To diagnose self in relation to business leaders and prepare Oneself with requisite skills, especially to identify and prepare a plan of action to overcome some of the critical weaknesses.
Assessing Business Potential of an Idea: Creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship, Sources of new ideas, Techniques for generating new ideas, Opportunity recognition and Assessment.
Managing Legal Aspects of a business: Forms of business entities and related Implications, winding up of accompany, Need for a lawyer. Intellectual Property Rights and Implications for Entrepreneur.

Developing the Business idea into a Business Plan: Business plan – what, when and for whom?, Business plan drivers, Pitching BP, Why plan fails? Various facets of BP - market, management team, financial requirements, risks involved, and exit strategy. Marketing Plan- Need and importance of marketing research, tools and techniques for undertaking market research. Operation and Production Plan – Product design & analysis, New product development, Product specifications and customer needs, Production, planning and control.

Incorporating Revenue model into Business: Basic financial modeling, Basic elements of finance, Understanding cash flow projection and budgeting, Balance sheets and income tax, Break-even analysis, ratio analysis.

Art of raising finance: Raising Finance, Assessing financial requirements, Issues in raising finance, Understanding the financers. Sources of finance - seed funding, angel funding, venture capitalist funding, raising money from banks, lease financing and financial institutions etc. Start up to Going Public: What is an IPO? When to go for IPO? Steps involved in issuing an IPO, Marketing strategies for IPO.

Art and science of Managing People: Venture team development, Building winning team, People management – key to success, organizational structure and systems, Designing an effective organizational structure.

Developing Business Strategy - Launching and Growth of Business: New Venture launch and Managing Early Growth, Steps involved in launching a business, Raising different resources, motivating and inspiring a team, Understanding technology trends, managing cash, Record keeping and due diligence, Implementation plan. Managing Growth - Venture development stages, Why entrepreneurs do not scale up?
Revival, Exit and End of a venture: Managing Change, Key strategies to turn around, liquidation, exit strategy for entrepreneur.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
about: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO. The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance. a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions. b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines. c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.

Prediction and Assessments of impacts of socio – economic and human health aspects

title: DISSERTATION
about: This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty member/professional. The course must end with a well defined Final Report outlining all the investigations, achievements and conclusions at the end of each semester. References and bibliography in standard format are also to be included in the report. The aim of this course is to carryout a research and development project in assigned areas of professional interest. The course envisages student’s training in the methodology of research and presentation of the research findings in the form of a scientific report. OPERATION OF THE COURSE The student should immediately chalk out a plan of work in Consultation with his Supervisor. Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating the intermediate milestones and the estimated time to achieve the same along with references and bibliography. Within two weeks of registration, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the Head of Department in TS-1 Performa. The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other faculty in relevant area may be requested to attend the presentations. Supervisor will announce the Mid-semester grade to his student and send the MID-SEM Evaluation Form to the Head of Department. Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to be submitted to the supervisor on or before the last day of class work in each semester. Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative arrangement made by the supervisor. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to the supervisor. The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for any genuine needs. A check-list of various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. OPERATION OF THE COURSE The student should immediately chalk out a plan of work in Consultation with his Supervisor. Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating the intermediate milestones and the estimated time to achieve the same along with references and bibliography. Within two weeks of registration, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the Head of Department in TS-1 Performa. The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other faculty in relevant area may be requested to attend the presentations. Supervisor will announce the Mid-semester grade to his student and send the MID-SEM Evaluation Form to the Head of Department. Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to be submitted to the supervisor on or before the last day of class work in each semester. Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative arrangement made by the supervisor. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to the supervisor. The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for any genuine needs. If leave of absence exceeds seven days in entire semester, recommended 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division final grade may be revised by su pervisor. The following format for Dissertation Abstract should be used. Abstract should also be Format for submission of Dissertation Abstract ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Semester: First/Second Session Abstract (Approx 1000 to 2000 words) A separate Dissertation topic has to be assigned to individual students. Wherever the broad area is same, the aspects to be researched by an individual candidate should be clearly focused and spelt out. Utmost care should be taken in the preparation of the FINAL REPORT. A check-list of various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. Supervisors are also requested to examine the draft of the FINAL REPORT keeping in view the items in the checklist. Title of the thesis should be proper and should be indicative of the type of work done.

title: SURVEYING
about: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these areas have also been included. The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced surveying techniques. Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses. Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination. Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction. Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations. Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods. Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks. Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications. Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data. Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software.

title: Fluid Mechanics
about: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels. Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. about: This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and nonuniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to fluid machinery. The problems encountered by our society, such as water supply, irrigation, navigation, and water power, resulted in the development of Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Engineering. The objective of this course is to equip students with a fundamental understanding of the principles of fluid mechanics as applied to hydraulic systems and structures. The course aims to achieve the following Course Objectives (Teacher's To develop an analytical understanding of flow behavior in pipes and channels under varying conditions. To apply fluid mechanics principles in analyzing hydraulic systems, including energy losses and force impacts. To introduce the working principles and performance of fluid machinery relevant to civil engineering. To prepare students for practical problem-solving in the analysis, design, and assessment of water infrastructures of Pipe networks, open channels, and structures submerged in fluid, like bridge piers, dealt with by civil engineers. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Explain the behaviour of real fluids, including boundary layer development and turbulent flow through conduits, and apply these concepts to practical hydraulic engineering problems. Analyze closed-conduit hydraulic systems by evaluating head losses, pipe flow characteristics, pumps, valves, fittings, and the effects of water hammer in pressurized pipelines. Analyze and solve pipe network problems using the Hardy Cross Method for the design and operation of water distribution systems. Analyze uniform and non-uniform flow in open channels using fundamental hydraulic principles and empirical equations for engineering design and performance assessment. Evaluate fluid forces on immersed bodies, including drag, lift, and the impact of jets on stationary and moving surfaces, for engineering applications. Explain the classification, operating principles, and applications of fluid machinery, particularly hydraulic turbines and pumps, and relate them to hydraulic engineering systems.

title: DESIGN OF REINFORCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
about: Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability; Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending; Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases. In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangularand T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.
topics: Concepts and Principles of Limit state Design
Analysis of beams and one-way slab for Flexure
Design of beams and one-way slab for Flexure
Design of Flexural members for Shear
Design of Flexural Members for Bond
Design of Flexural members for Limit State of Serviceability

title: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering
about: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering. Introduction to in-situ testing, drilling, and sampling, advantages and disadvantages of in-situ testing, and scope of using the test results for direct and indirect design of geotechnical structures. Learn about SPT, test procedure, SPT corrections, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. Become familiar with some of the frequently used methods for the design of foundations using SPT data. Learn about CPT, test procedure, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. Design of foundations based on CPT results. Assess liquefaction potential for a site based on SPT and CPT results. Estimate seismic wave velocities and interpret subsurface profiles based on seismic reflection and refraction tests, and SASW test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs based on exploration findings will be discussed. Remember different in-situ testing methods related to geotechnical engineering. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Understanding of different widely used in-situ testing procedures and principles pertaining to geotechnical engineering. Knowledge of appropriate correlation equations available to interpret different geomaterial properties using in-situ test results. Apply different direct design methods for designing foundations. Analyze and compare different in-situ test results for tests conducted at the same site and decide suitability of different test methods. Evaluate the suitability of different test methods based on site details and purpose of testing, select suitable method for foundation design using in-situ test results and assess potential for liquefaction.

title: Fundamentals of Systems Engineering
about: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments. The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning. a. Understand systems engineering principles and their application to infrastructure life-cycle management. b. Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex infrastructure systems. c. Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure planning and operations. d. Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment analysis methods. e. Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into infrastructure systems design and management.
topics: Introduction to basics of System Engineering and related approaches
Solving System Engineering problems using Linear Programming, Queuing theory, and
Network scheduling, resource planning and financial management
Application of AI, IoT, Robotics in Civil Engineering systems

title: Water Resources Planning and Management
about: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making. a. Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems. b. Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project evaluation. c. Analyze point and non-point source pollution using water quality modeling techniques. d. Assess groundwater resources and apply methods for sustainable groundwater management. e. Perform statistical and uncertainty analyses related to streamflow and water availability. f. Formulate and solve water resource problems using linear, non-linear, and multi-objective optimization techniques. g. Plan and manage reservoir operations under both deterministic and stochastic environments. h. Utilize modern tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence in water resource management. Evaluate real-world case studies and apply integrated approaches to address complex water management challenges.
topics: Water Resource systems and role of modeling, planning and management: An Overview
Water Resource Systems: Its Role in Planning and Management
Integrated water resource planning and conservation
Models for Identifying and Evaluating Alternatives
Optimization Models and Methods in Water Resource Systems
Applications in Water Resources Planning and Management

about: The course deals with planning techniques, engineering economy, valuation including estimation & costing, system design, construction methodologies ranging from small buildings to large infrastructure projects, construction technologies including recent advancements. Relevant Indian Standard codes of practices will be given emphasis. The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of construction planning and management right from the knowledge of various activities till the estimation, costing, valuation, tendering etc., Though this course covers wider infrastructure projects, the primary focus will be on building and road infrastructure. To understand the different construction projects and basic objective of project management [Module I] To understand the project management techniques (CPM and PERT) [Module - II] To analyze the various requirements of manpower and other resources [ Module-III] To analyze the various control methodologies keeping in line with project requirements [Module-IV] To get exposed to construction contracts and tenders [Module-V] To estimate the quantity and rate of different building components (including materials) [Module VI] To discuss the various aspects of valuation of properties [Module VII] To highlights various aspects of construction quality and safety with case studies [Module VIII] To understand the best practices of construction management [Module IX] _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division The students will be trained to Demonstrate a systematic understanding of the function of project management in property, construction, and the project lifecycle; and of the concepts, theories, principles, and techniques associated with construction project management at strategic and operational level. Critically apply established techniques of analysis and enquiry to construction project management and use judgement to evaluate a range of solutions. Provide appropriate construction management advice to organizations in order to meet objectives while meeting required standards of ethics and governance. Demonstrate the skills to manage procedures and processes during the construction project lifecycle. Understand the legal implications of contract, common, and regulatory law to manage a construction project

Project Management with CPM and PERT
Real time project networking of big infrastructure projects.
Project construction equipment including selection of equipment

title: Pavement Material Characterization
about: [as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example. The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different lectures. a. . To characterize pavement materials b. . To perform bituminous mix design c. . To perform mix design of concrete

title: AIRPORT PLANNING & DESIGN
about: The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc., The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of airport planning and design.
