title: Advanced Algorithms & Complexity
about: To learn about some Probability Theory that is applied in Algorithm Design and Analysis and Computational Complexity. To learn about some applications of Probability Theory in Game Theory Parallel Algorithms Distributed Algorithms Number Theoretic Algorithms To learn about some applications of Probability Theory in Deterministic Complexity Classes: P, NP, PSPACE, #P Randomized Complexity Classes: BPP, RP, co-RP, ZPP Interactive Proofs Probabilistically Checkable Proofs
topics: Polynomial Time Reductions. The Complexity Classes NP- Complete and NP-Hard. The Satisfiability Problem.
NP-Completeness of 3SAT, 0/1 Integer Programming and Independent Set.
The Complexity Classes PSPACE and NPSPACE.
PSPACE-Completeness of True Quantified Boolean Formulas.
Probability, Random Variables and Expectation. Linearity of Expectation.
The Randomized Complexity Classes BPP, RP, co-RP and ZPP.
Markov’s Inequality, Chebyshev’s Inequality and Chernoff’s Bounds.
Atlantic City, Monte Carlo and Las Vegas Algorithms.
QBF Games. Deterministic Game Tree Evaluation Algorithms.
Randomized Game Tree Evaluation Algorithms. Game Theory.
Application of Minimax Theorems in Proving Lower Bounds for Game Tree Evaluation.

EREW PRAM Algorithm for Maximal Independent Sets.
Extended Euclid’s Algorithm for GCD and its Complexity.
Congruences. Fermat’s Little Theorem. Euler’s Theorem.
Modular Exponentiation using Repeated Squaring. Wilson’s Theorem.
Legendre’s Symbol. Randomized Algorithm for finding Square Roots Modulo a Prime.
Interactive Proofs. Interactive Proof for Graph Non Isomorphism. Interactive Proof for Quadratic Non Residuosity.
Arthur-Merlin Proofs and Merlin-Arthur Proofs. Pairwise Independent Hash Functions.
Interactive Proof for Set Lower Bound. GNI \in AM[2].
Approximation Algorithms for NP-Hard Optimization Problems.
Probabilistically Checkable Proofs. PCP Theorem and Locally Testable Proofs. PCP Theorem and Hardness of
Equivalence of the “Proof View” and the “Hardness of Approximation View” of the PCP Theorem.
Hardness of Approximation for Vertex Cover and Independent Set.

about: The primary objective of the course is to introduce the student to cloud computing from architectural and design perspectives. As such, the emphasis of the course would be on the underlying infrastructure and architecture of clouds, techniques for enabling services and the quality of such services, as well as issues in designing clouds. Select research issues in performance, security, and management would also be addressed. Programming on the cloud would be encouraged but not taught in class. Students are expected to learn and understand tools and techniques for using, designing, and implementing clouds and services via assignments and a term project.
topics: Evolution of Computing Systems – Mainframes to PCs to Networked Systems to Clouds. Introduction to Cloud Computing – NIST definition, enablers and economies of scale.
Introduction to Cloud Computing – product vs process, service orientation of a process, computing as a utility.
Introduction to Cloud Computing – Service delivery models, cloud deployment models with examples.
Service Level Agreements (SLAs), Service Level Objectives (SLOs); Availability: high availability models, measurement
Scalability: Principles and techniques; Scaling services: Web services; Micro services; Elasticity
In-memory Distributed Programming: Spark; Stream processing on cluster: Storm.
Virtualization: Introduction, Different Levels of Abstraction, and Mechanisms for Virtualization. Process vs. System VMs, HLL VMs.
System VMs: ISA Virtualizability and Resource Virtualization – CPU
System VMs: Virtualization of Memory (VMWare) and I/O
Para virtualization: Xen; Hardware-assisted virtualization: Intel VT
Hardware building blocks of a cloud data center: compute, storage, network; challenges in storage and networking
Workloads and software infrastructure in a cloud datacenter
Network virtualization: Datacenter network topologies; Routing solutions; SDN
Storage virtualization: NAS and SAN, Virtual Storage; SDN
Distributed storage: file systems, databases, challenges in scaling, challenges in distributed storage
Distributed storage: replication vs partitioning, leaderless replication; Dynamo; S3
Data partitioning: approaches, balancing partitions, request routing
Data replication: consistency models, consensus through 2PC, 3PC, Paxos, active vs passive replication
Consensus in the cloud: ZAB, raft protocols; Zookeeper
Large scale distributed file systems: GFS, Ceph FS
Cloud databases: Cap theorem, PACELC theorem; NoSQL Databases
Security issues specific to cloud computing and solutions to address them.

title: Reconfigurable Computing
about: Overview of Programmable Logics. FPGA fabric architectures. Logic Elements and Switch Networks. Design and Synthesis of Combinational and Sequential Elements. Placement and Routing. Pipelining and other Design Methodologies. Fine-grained and Coarse-Grained FPGAs. Static and Dynamic Reconfiguration. Partitioning. Hardware/Software Partitioning and Partial Evaluation; Systolic Architectures. Users perspective of reconfigurability – implementation and use cases on modern FPGAs. Reconfigurable (adaptive) computing is a novel yet important research field investigating the capability of hardware to adapt to changing computational requirements such as emerging standards, late design changes, and even to changing processing requirements arising at run-time. Reconfigurable computing thus benefits from a) the programmability of software similar to the Von Neumann computer and b) the speed and efficiency of parallel hardware execution.The purpose of the course reconfigurable computing is to instruct students about the possibilities and rapidly growing interest in adaptive hardware and corresponding design techniques by providing them the necessary knowledge for understanding and designing reconfigurable hardware systems and studying applications benefiting from dynamic hardware reconfiguration. CO1: Identify the role and advantages of reconfigurable computing compared to other computing paradigms. CO2: Understand FPGA design flow, placement, routing, and configuration aspects in reconfigurable systems. CO3: Understand reconfiguration techniques such as partial and run-time reconfiguration in adaptive hardware systems. CO4: Apply Verilog to model and implement digital designs on FPGA platforms.
topics: Permanently Programmed FPGAs Programmable I/O, Circuit Design of FPGA Fabrics, Architecture of FPGA Fabrics, Case Studies (Xilinx/Altera/Microsemi/Actel).
Fine - Grained and Course - Grained Reconfigurable Architecture, Case Studies.
Logic Implementation for FPGAs, Syntax- Directed Translation Logic Synthesis
Multi-Level Logic Synthesis LUT- Based Technology Mapping
DFG, CFG Introduction to Binding, Scheduling and Allocation, Temporal Partitioning Temporal Partitioning Algorithms
Offline and Online Temporal Placement Routing Cost, Routing- Conscious Placement
Communication at run-time between modules on
Multi-Context FPGAs, Introduction to Partial Reconfiguration, rotecting the FPGA design from common threats, Design security concerns, Secure architecture in FPGAs and SoC FPGAs.

title: Agentic AI
about: Introduction to Transformers; advanced architectures beyond Transformers (state space models/Mamba, mixture-of-experts, diffusion-based language models); Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) Basics (LoRA), advanced PEFT (QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA, quantization-aware adapters); inference and decoding (top-k, top-p, beam, contrastive; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAttention, AWQ); Model quantization, pruning, distillation, on-device edge optimization; test-time compute (self-consistency, Tree, Graph-of-Thought); post-training & alignment (Reinforcement DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO; rejection sampling, instruction tuning, distillation, tool & function calling, Model Context Protocol (MCP)); Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Basics, Advanced RAG (IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy); Agent Security (threat models, attack mechanisms and defense strategies, red teaming, blue teaming);evolutionary/genetic methods (prompt & agent evolution); multimodal LLMs & agents (Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA; MM-ReAct, ViperGPT). Compare and justify LLM/agent architecture choices for long-context, latency, and reasoning. Implement and evaluate PEFT methods under memory/compute constraints. Design decoding and test-time compute strategies within fixed latency/cost budgets. Build and align models/agents using RLHF and direct-alignment methods; diagnose reward hacking and length bias. Construct robust, programmable RAG agent pipelines with provenance and corrective feedback. Analyze and mitigate AI agent security threats, conduct red & blue teaming. Apply evolutionary search to improve prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies. Fine-tune and evaluate multimodal LLMs/agents; integrate perception with tool-use plans safely. 1 Explain and compare advanced LLM/agent architectures (Transformers, SSMs, Mamba, MoE, diffusion etc.). Apply parameter–efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA) under memory and compute constraints. Configure decoding and serving (top-k, top-p, beam; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAttention) to meet latency and cost targets. Implement test-time compute strategies (self-consistency, Tree/Graph-of-Thought) and evaluate accuracy–cost trade-offs. Build post-training model/agent pipelines (SFT → reward modeling → RLHF or direct alignment) and mitigate reward hacking/length bias. Use direct-alignment methods (DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO) and rejection sampling to improve helpfulness and safety. Design robust RAG agentic systems (IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy) with provenance and corrective feedback. Evaluate and defend AI agents against adversarial threats (prompt injection, data poisoning, tool misuse); perform red & blue teaming. Employ evolutionary methods to optimize prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies against defined fitness metrics. Fine-tune and assess multimodal LLMs/agents (e.g., LLaVA, MM-ReAct) with appropriate safety guardrails.
topics: Beyond Transform- ers I: State Space Models, Mixture of Experts&Diffusion- based Language Models
Advanced PEFT and Model Com- pression: PEFT Basics, LoRA, QLoRA, & DoRA, AdaLoRA and Q- awareLoRA
Post-Training II: PPO/REINFORCE, GRPO, Rejection Sampling
Post-Training III: Direct Alignment (DPO family), In- struction Tuning, Tools
Advanced RAG I: RAG Basics, IR Foundations to HyDE/RAPTOR
Evolutionary & Ge- netic Methods with LLMs

Fine-tune and assess multimodal LLMs/agents (e.g., LLaVA, MM-ReAct) with appropriate safety guardrails.

title: Introduction to Python
about: Introduction to Python, analysis of the problem, design, implementation, and testing, Python programming fundamentals: program structure, data types, variables, expressions, assignment; Program control statements: if, else, logical operators, assignment operators, conditional operators, blocks. Program repetition statements: while, for; Data Structures: Lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries; Using functions: writing functions enhance program modularity; String handling, File handling, Exception handling, Object-oriented fundamentals: classes, objects, methods, abstraction, predefined classes; Writing classes: programmer-defined classes, instance data and methods, parameters, overloading, encapsulation. Python programming is an essential skill that is increasingly relevant in today’s technologydriven world. This course is designed to introduce students to the core concepts of Python programming, guiding them through essential topics such as problem analysis, design, implementation, and testing. Students will gain hands-on experience with Python programming fundamentals, including program structure, data types, variables, and expressions. The course will cover key programming concepts such as control statements (if, else, logical and conditional operators), repetition statements (while, for loops), and data structures (lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries). By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and skills to write Python programs from scratch, design custom classes, and apply core programming techniques to real-world problems. title: Computational Thinking & Programming
about: Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design, functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers, dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and verification of generated code. Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory; file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted code. This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail, express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution. Express computational problems using abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and structured representations including flowcharts and pseudocode. Implement programs using fundamental constructs including variables, data types, conditionals, iteration, and modular function design. Apply recursion and dynamic memory management to solve problems involving structured and linked data representations. Implement file handling operations for sequential data processing and structured input/output.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
about: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that seeks to build systems that emulate human cognition. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities that mimic human intelligence, such as problem-solving, reasoning, planning, uncertainty handling, and learning. The course introduces students to a large collection of algorithms and techniques for building these intelligent entities. By the end of the course, the students should have a general knowledge of the field of AI. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve problems. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter. This course covers the issues and techniques involved in creating computer systems that exhibit intelligent behavior. The following are among the topics that we will cover: AI search techniques, Game Playing, Planning, Knowledge Representation, Reasoning under Uncertainty, and Reinforcement Learning.

title: Deep Learning
about: In the last decade, due to the availability of cheap computational power and relevant software tools, several neural networks are explored to advance state-of-the-art of many hard AI problems. These architectures have successfully advanced various areas such as image searching, natural language understanding, medical applications, autonomous vehicles etc. All these problems rely on efficient, accurate and robust solutions for basic vision tasks like image classification, localization and detection. In this course students will be given an exposure to the details of neural networks as well as deep learning architectures and to develop end-to-end models for such tasks. Students will learn to implement, train and debug their own neural networks. This is a project oriented practical course in which every student has to develop a complete working model to solve some real world problem. title: Information Retrieval
about: This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental evaluation. title: Product Design
about: The course covers various approaches to designing and developing a successful product. User research, requirements analysis, problem-specific creative solution-finding, costing, synthesis and analysis of design are included. Modularization necessary for administering large design exercises and design decision-making processes, is deliberated. Concepts of value engineering, Engineering ethics, and Design for X, along with case studies, are also incorporated. This course is designed to impart the knowledge required to develop a new product – understand the opportunity, develop a concept, and implement a concept. After the successful completion of this course, students shall be able to understand and use the various processes, tools and techniques required for designing a product: product specification development; concept generation, concept selection, concept testing and embodiment; product architecture; industrial design; design for X; analytical and numerical models; physical prototypes, models and experimentation; environmental, economic and social issues in product development; patents and intellectual properties.

title: Electrical Machines
about: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts. title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
about: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Communication Systems
about: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

title: Electromagnetic Fields and Microwave Engineering
about: Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric Waveguides; Cavity resonator, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices (Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; Microwave Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to analyze electromagnetic wave propagation using Maxwell’s equations, understand wave behavior at interfaces, and design transmission lines with impedance matching using the Smith Chart. They will gain proficiency in characterizing waveguides, cavity resonators, and microwave devices, as well as interpreting Sparameters for network analysis. Students will also learn measurement techniques, explore microwave sources and amplifiers, and evaluate various antenna types and their radiation characteristics for practical applications.

about: This course is a foundation course for the students entering into the discipline of Economics & Finance. This introductory course teaches the basic concepts related to the economic system that are listed as follows: Introduction to Economics (Microeconomics) & Economic Problems; Demand, Supply, & Elasticity; Household Behavior and Consumer choice; The Production Process; Costs and Output Decisions; Demand for Production Inputs; Market Imperfections: Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic Competition; Introduction to Macroeconomics and the Problems; Measurement of National Income & Output; Money Supply and the Banking System The main objective is to introduce the fundamental concepts and tools necessary to acquire an understanding of economic decision making of market participants such as Individual households, firms, and the government. The course covers two major areas of economics namely Microeconomics and Macroeconomics. The knowledge of the fundamentals would help the students to better understand the entire economic system and the process followed in policy making. This course would lay foundation for the students to understand other related courses in economics & finance such as Mathematical Economics, International Economics, Advance Micro and Macroeconomics, among others.

title: Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting
about: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance. The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company. Students who complete this course would be able to a. Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions. b. Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. c. Identify the financial position and performance of the companies. d. Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS
about: The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into two parts: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regression analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses, and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical Inference: Introduction to Probability and its distributions, sampling distributions, theory of estimation, Tests of Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non-Parametric); and Mathematical Methods include Concepts from Linear Algebra & their Applications (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory); Concepts from Calculus and their applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications. The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory. Apply appropriate methods for data collection, sampling, organization, and descriptive analysis, using graphical and numerical techniques to summarize and interpret statistical data. Analyze relationships among economic and business variables using correlation and regression techniques, and construct and interpret index numbers for relevant applications. Analyze time-series data by identifying its components, understanding the underlying data-generating process, and assessing stationarity. Apply probability concepts and statistical inference techniques, including probability and sampling distributions, estimation, and parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, to draw valid conclusions from data. Apply mathematical methods to economic problems, using concepts from linear algebra, input-output analysis, game theory, calculus, and optimization to formulate and solve economic decision problems.

title: ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS
about: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure. The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context. This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically. Understanding L.1.1. about: This course develops a systematic exposition of both classical and modern theories of international trade in goods and services that try to explain the composition, direction, and consequences of international trade, and the determinants and effects of trade policy. It then builds on the models of open economy macroeconomics.  To understand the effects of international trade on individuals and businesses  To understand the effects of changes in trade policies on trade  To apply macroeconomic models to understand the international economy.  To focus on the interrelationships among aggregate economic variables such as GDP, unemployment rates, inflation rates, trade balances, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.  To focus on the significance of trade imbalances, the determinants of exchange rates, and the aggregate effects of government monetary and fiscal policies.

title: ISSUES IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
about: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping longrun development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development. The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to realworld economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. 1 Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani Pilani | Dubai | Goa | Hyderabad ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION Explain and critically evaluate the major theories, concepts, and contemporary issues in development economics, including economic growth, structural transformation, poverty, inequality, employment, human development, institutional change, globalization, environmental sustainability, and emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and digital transformation. Apply appropriate analytical, quantitative, and empirical tools to interpret development indicators, assess the effectiveness of development policies and programmes, and evaluate alternative strategies for promoting sustainable, inclusive, and equitable economic development at national and international levels. Critically analyze contemporary development challenges using theoretical and empirical evidence, formulate evidence-based policy recommendations, and undertake independent research on key issues affecting developing economies, with particular reference to India and other emerging economies.

title: Financial Management
about: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.

about: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA). Prerequisites: This is an elementary course on Derivatives and Risk Management and does not assume any prior knowledge of Financial Markets, Instruments and Derivatives. However, familiarity of basic economic theory such as law of supply and demand, utility maximization principle, compounding and discounting of cash flows, etc. are desirable. The course is not mathematically rigorous and a first-year course on elementary linear algebra, calculus, probability, and differential equations will be sufficient to grasp the contents of the course. It is expected that students have technical know-how of MS excel as it will be used to demonstrate required computations, wherever required, and for carrying out take-home assignments. title: BUSINESS ANALYSIS AND VALUATION
about: This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking in business valuation and decision-making. The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions. The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of financial analysis, advanced accounting practices, and valuation techniques. By the end of the program, learners will be able to effectively analyze financial statements, gaining insights into an organization's performance and financial health. A critical component of the curriculum focuses on valuation methods, where students will learn to assess the value of assets and investments using various approaches, such as discounted cash flow analysis and market comparables. This knowledge will empower them to evaluate investment opportunities critically and make informed decisions that can significantly impact an organization's financial strategy. Overall, these outcomes will prepare students for successful careers in finance and accounting, equipping them with both analytical and practical skills essential for navigating complex financial landscapes.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
about: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance. Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. Technical analysis. Financial derivative contracts and their applications. Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio. Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests. Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return. Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance. Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed. Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change.

title: New Venture Creation
about: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guestlectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business. NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?

title: Urban Water Management
about: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions. The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.  Understand and assess the urban water cycle and system interactions under climate change and urbanization.  Demonstrate practical knowledge in water quality, stormwater, and sanitation system design and management.  Use hydroinformatics and modeling tools for flood forecasting and system performance evaluation.  Integrate water-sensitive urban design principles and sustainability indicators in planning.

title: Electrical Machines
about: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machinesuniversal motors, Induction generators. Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts. The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
about: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Communication Systems
about: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
about: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, areaefficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces. ⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic. ⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design. ⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential. ⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference Circuit. ⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs. ⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout. ⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments. ⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels of design abstraction. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGSD/ AGSRD Division

title: FPGA BASED SYSTEM DESIGN
about: Digital system design options and trade-offs, design methodology and technology overview, Programmable Logic Devices, SPLDs, CPLDs, and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs); FPGA architectural options, granularity of function and wiring resources, coarse vs. fine-grained, vendor-specific issues (emphasis on Xilinx and Altera), Logic fabric, Look-up tables, block BRAMs, DSP slices etc., timing models, power dissipation, Input and Output cell characteristics, clock input, Timing, Power dissipation, Programmable interconnect, Hardware Description Languages, FPGA system design tools, synthesis, and implementation, design verification and debugging, FPGA based design studies, interfacing with input-output devices and data converters.  Build a strong foundation in FPGA architecture, technologies, and design methodologies.  Develop proficiency in HDL-based design for creating complex digital systems.  Explore the full FPGA design flow—from concept to implementation and debugging.  Integrate embedded processors, IP cores, and DSP functions into FPGA-based designs.  Apply knowledge through hands-on labs and projects using modern FPGA platforms. Students will gain a comprehensive understanding of FPGA architecture and design flow, develop proficiency in HDL-based digital design, and learn to integrate digital system, embedded processors, and IP cores. They will also acquire hands-on experience with modern FPGA tools and platforms to implement, debug, and optimize complex digital systems.

title: Internet of Things
about: Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL). This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT systems and make end-toend solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world problems. a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation.
topics: Introduction to IoT & Cyber-Physical Systems, IoT applications - an overview, Different Levels of IoT Applications: Level 1 - 6 with examples, IoT Design Methodology & Life Cycle, Introduction to IoT Physical End Points & Platforms, IoT System Design Examples (for applications like fitness tracker, smart parking etc.). Learning these concepts to understand how end to end IoT applications work.

Introduction to sensors for IoT application development, Data Acquisition, Signal Conditioning and Processing, Multi Sensor fusion for IoT, Advanced sensing techniques (e.g. BCI/HCI), Actuators and Controllers for IoT. Understand their working and how to apply them to develop novel technology solutions

Introduction to Arduino microcontroller & NodeMCU for IoT applications, Programming with Arduino & NodeMCU and prototype development (e.g. for smart farming, smart city applications etc.), Introduction to Raspberry Pi, Programming Raspberry Pi (Python), Rest API based hands on. Getting a hands on experience in these tools to enhance skill set.

Understanding wireless sensor networks: Introduction, Deployment, Localization, Routing, MAC, Time synchronization and Multi-sensor-fusion for WSN. Blockchain fundamentals and it’s applications in IoT
Get an overview of Ad Hoc networks (MANET, VANET, FANET), Industrial IoT Networks, Common network standards (Bluetooth, NFC, LORA) etc, COAP and MQTT (including lab/ hands-on)

Understanding data management for IoT, Advanced optimization for processing sensor data, Machine learning for IoT data analytics, Introduction to IoT Cloud Services, Case studies of Cloud services for IoT and learning how to use them.
Get an overview of cyber-attacks on IoT- Case study and understand security solutions for IoT: hardware/software

title: Modern Control Systems
about: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the socalled Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains. Scopes and Objectives After completing this course the students will be able to Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones Prescribed Text/ Reference Books Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus

title: Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics
about: Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electrooptic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks. In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.  CLO1: Basic configuration of a fiber-optic system, Merits of Fiber Optic system, Ray propagation through different types of optical fibers and Estimation of different parameters of optical fibers.  CLO2: Familiarization with the background for learning of electromagnetic wave propagation in medium, Modal analysis of planar optical wave guides, Modal analysis of cylindrical optical waveguide and characterization of optical fibers.  CLO3: Concept of semi-conductor p-n junction towards design LED, LED designs characterization and ILD condition for laser action, Optical transmitter design and applications  CLO4: Basic principle of opto-electronic detection, Types of photodiodes, Structures of photodetectors and optical receivers, Operation of Optical Amplifiers, Optical modulators and demodulators.  CLO5: Optical Communication system design for single wavelength and multi wavelength systems. Design of fiber optic sensors, Extrinsic and Intrinsic Sensors Distinct Types of Sensors and their Industrial Applications Text Book (TB): Khare, R.P.: “Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics” Oxford University Press (2004) Reference Book (RB): Keiser, G., "Optical Fiber Communications", 5/e, McGraw Hill, 2013 Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division

title: Digital Image Processing
about: This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition. Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology.

title: Semiconductor Fabrication Technology
about: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail. This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines.

title: Satellite Communications
about: Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO, MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications. This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, orbital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and linkbudget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixedassignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit. Some of the key learning outcomes are stated below. Explain the fundamental concepts, historical evolution, segments, and subsystems of satellite communication systems. Analyze radio-wave propagation effects and orbital mechanics (LEO/MEO/GEO) and their influence on system and link design. Design and evaluate satellite RF uplink/downlink link budgets, including noise and intermodulation considerations, using hand calculations and simulation tools. 1 Apply and compare digital modulation, coding, and multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) for satellite systems. Identify and evaluate VSAT, mobile satellite links, understand GPS/GNSS system architectures and their performance limitations To understand, appreciate and analyze recent trends in satellite communications such as next generation non-terrestrial network/space-air-ground integrated network.
