title: Machine Learning for Electronics Engineers
about: The rise of machine learning (ML) has introduced many opportunities in the design of electronic systems. This course provides a requisite conceptual foundation of ML and contextual application of ML techniques for improving the performance of electronic systems. The course introduces the major approaches to ML such as supervised, unsupervised, semisupervised, and reinforcement learning. The course also lays emphasis on various deep learning techniques and their application to various types of electronic systems/sub-systems (e.g. control-dominated systems, NLP systems, vision-based systems, communication systems, embedded systems, IoTs). Additionally, the course covers advance topics in ML such as multimodal, multi-task learning as well as transfer learning. The course discusses the challenges in implementation of ML techniques, complexity analysis of the ML architectures for hardware implementation, efficient architectures, and various topologies used for implementation. Students should be able to apply ML techniques to model, design, validate, and optimize embedded electronic systems in their area of interest. Develop the skills and practical exposure in modeling, developing, and debugging MLbased systems. Develop the foundation required to explore advanced topics of research in ML.

title: Real-Time Embedded Systems
about: This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc.

title: Signal Theory and Optimization
about: Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes; vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition; matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and numerical optimization techniques. The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties, limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables. The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques. The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random signals and related theory, ii) linear algebra, matrices iii) optimization techniques and their uses in communications and signal processing. At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided next generation communication networks.

Characteristic function, properties, Useful inequalities, Central limit theorem, applications, examples
Random variables (Contd.,): transformation of random variables, generation and simulation of random variables, simulation of random variables, multiple random variables
Stochastic processes: Specifying random process, types of random process, wide sense stationarity (WSS), ergodicity, transmission of random process, examples, applications
Convex and non-convex optimization: key techniques, limitations and few applications

title: Modelling and Analysis of Electrical Machines
about: Review of Rotating Electrical Machines, Element of Generalized Theory of Rotating Electrical Machines, Linear transformation and Reference-frame Theory, DC Machines, Three-phase Synchronous Machines, Three-phase Induction Machines, Special Machines, Introduction to motor parameters estimation and model generation using MATLAB The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state, transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive maintenance, and advanced control. The prerequisite of this course is, to have a basic understanding of electrical circuits, electrical machines and control systems; mainly modelling of physical systems. Students will be able to, a. Develop the model of electrical machines using actual machine variables and parameters. b. Develop generalized theory (unified approach) based model of electrical machines. c. Apply different transformations using reference frame theory to simplify machine modelling. d. Develop the block-diagram of electrical machines using their dynamic model. e. Develop and visualize machine-model using software such as MATLAB-Simulink, and use the model for analysis and control-loop design for hardware testing and implementation using real-time simulators such as TMS320F28379d.
topics: Recap of electrical machines and basic principles of analysis
Commonly used reference frame and transformation between them.
Conventional modelling using system variables, state equations, transfer functions, block-diagram
Generalized theory based modelling of separately excited dc generator and motor, series and shunt motor
Machine parameters, voltage/torque equations, and their reference frame variables
Steady-state, Short-circuit, transients and dynamic analysis
Dynamic performance at torque change and three-phase fault
Equivalent circuit, Voltage and torque equations
Dynamic performance analysis at torque change and three-phase fault
Basics of VSI drives steady-state and average values modelling and analysis

title: EEE G554
about: This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-currentswitching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course. a. Understand the concept of resonant tank network b. Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance c. Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter d. Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching
topics: Series, parallel, series-parallel resonant DC-DC converters, half and full bridge topologies, analysis and design
Sinusoidal analysis of resonant converters, analysis and design
Operation of the Full Bridge Below Resonance: ZCS, ZVS
Inverter output characteristics, Dependence of Transistor Current on Load, Dependence of the ZVS/ZCS Boundary on Load Resistance, Example of LLC tank, Results for Basic Tank Networks

title: Power Quality
about: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises. A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems. Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.
topics: Power Quality Applications and Related Topics

title: NANO-ELECTRONICS AND NANO-PHOTONICS TECHNOLOGY
about: Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology. This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.
topics: (L30-33) Optical sensors, devices and nonlinear operations

title: Advanced Wireless Communications
about: Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless networks, D2D communicationsmodeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in wireless communications. This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the nextgeneration wireless networks. The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless communications. New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready. Evaluate the trade-offs in system design parameters (e.g., power, bandwidth, latency, mobility) in the context of modern wireless networks. Design and evaluate advanced modulation, coding, and diversity techniques for improving link reliability and spectral efficiency in various wireless environments. Analyze complex wireless channel models (e.g., time-varying fading, spatially correlated MIMO channels) and assess their implications on communication system performance.
topics: Mathematical tools for wireless network analysis
D2D communications, modulation, and multiple access schemes

title: Advanced Digital Communication
about: Introduction to digital communication systems; signal characterization and representation of bandpass and low-pass signals; signal space analysis; fundamentals of source coding and entropy; digital modulation techniques and constellation design; optimum receivers for additive white Gaussian noise channels; maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection; symbol error probability analysis; non-coherent detection methods; carrier and symbol synchronization techniques; communication over band-limited channels; ISI, Nyquist criteria, and signal waveform design, equalization; multicarrier modulation systems, effects of intercarrier interference (ICI) and carrier frequency offset (CFO); channel capacity limits and fundamentals of channel coding. To provide fundamental knowledge to model, design, and analyze advanced digital communication systems, with applications in both industry and R&D. To reinforce theoretical concepts through practical assignments using MATLAB, Python, and USRP. Requires prior knowledge of Linear Systems, Probability Theory, Stochastic Processes, and basic Communication Systems.
topics: 1-2: Principles of communication, elements of digital communication system, sources of information, communication channels and their characteristics, modulation process, history of digital communication
3-5: Signal spaces, inner product and orthogonal expansion, Gram Schmitt orthogonalization, bandpass/lowpass signal representation
6-9: Coding of analog sources, Memoryless modulation – PAM, phase modulation, quadrature amplitude modulation, FSK, PPM, bi-orthogonal modulation, simplex signal set; Modulation with memory – CPFSK
10-13: Correlation demodulator, matched filter demodulator, optimum detector, ML detector, MAP detector.
14-20: Error probabilities for band limited signaling, power limited signaling, optimal detection in presence of uncertainty – non coherent detection
21-23: Signal parameter estimation, carrier phase estimation, symbol timing estimation – early late gate synchronizers
24-30: Signal design for band limited channels, probability of error for zero ISI and system design in the presence of channel distortion, equalizer design
31-33: Fundamentals of source coding, entropy, and data compression.
Understanding multicarrier systems, their modulation and demodulation methods

title: Hardware and Software Codesign
about: This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. This course also teaches analysis and optimization processes for supporting algorithmic and architectural design decisions. It also helps the student gain design experience through different case studies. The course emphasizes a top-down design methodology driven by bottom-up constraints. The topics covered will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and optimization. Course Learning Objectives (CLOs) are as follows a. Analyze embedded system requirements and develop suitable hardware–software co-design solutions by applying system-level modeling, partitioning, and synthesis techniques. b. Evaluate and optimize hardware–software architectures using partitioning algorithms, mapping strategies, and performance estimation methods to satisfy design constraints such as speed, area, power, and cost. c. Design and implement hardware–software co-designed embedded applications using contemporary design methodologies and FPGA-based platforms to address real-world engineering problems.
topics: Case study to understand Hardware Software codesign
KL Algorithm for partitioning, Simulated annealing etc.

title: Modern Control Systems
about: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the socalled Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains. Scopes and Objectives After completing this course the students will be able to Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones Prescribed Text/ Reference Books Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus

This course introduces the foundational principles of fluid mechanics and their practical applications in hydraulic systems used in water and wastewater treatment plants and sewerage networks. It covers the behavior of fluids in motion and at rest, emphasizing both theoretical frameworks and engineering applications. Topics include flow regimes, pressure losses, open channel flow, pump performance, and hydraulic modeling. Students will develop analytical skills to solve real-world fluid flow problems and design efficient hydraulic systems. Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics: Understand physical dimensions, units, and dimensionless analysis using Rayleigh and Buckingham π methods; Grasp the concept of hydraulic similarity and model testing Fluid Properties and Flow Regimes: Analyze dynamic and kinematic viscosity; Distinguish between laminar and turbulent flow using Reynolds experiment and Reynolds number. Flow in Pipes: Apply Poiseuille’s law for laminar flow pressure drop; Analyze velocity profiles and pressure loss in laminar and turbulent pipe flow; Use Moody diagram and Darcy’s law to determine friction factors. Complex Pipe Flow Systems: Evaluate flow in non-horizontal and variable diameter pipes; Estimate minor losses due to expansions, contractions, and fittings. Pipeline Flow Between Reservoirs: Assess head losses and solve problems involving series and parallel pipelines. Open Channel Flow: Define hydraulic parameters like wetted perimeter and hydraulic mean depth; Use Chezy’s and Manning’s equations to calculate discharge and flow depth. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Pumps and Hydraulic Machinery: Under stand types of rotodynamic pumps and their applications; Analyze pump performance, derive affinity laws, and interpret characteristic curves; Evaluate system losses and pump operation in series and parallel configurations.

title: Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology
about: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. Learning Objectives The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and geosphere. Learning objectives for each of the broad topics as discussed in the course plan has been described along with – what the learner should be able to do by studying these.

Foundations of Environmental Science and Biodiversity
Microbial Physiology, Metabolism, and Genetic Engineering
Bioremediation, Pollution Control, and Environmental Monitoring

title: Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting
about: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance. The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company. Students who complete this course would be able to a. Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions. b. Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. c. Identify the financial position and performance of the companies. d. Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
about: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance. Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. Technical analysis. Financial derivative contracts and their applications. Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio. Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests. Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return. Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance. Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed. Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change.

Introduction to Options, Futures, Forwards, derivatives trading mechanics, pay-off diagrams, application of derivatives in hedging and speculation

title: Financial Management
about: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.

title: Financial Risk Analytics and Management
about: This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives. The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document. a. Understand and classify financial risks such as interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk, and portfolio risk in modern financial markets. b. Analyze and implement risk measurement tools such as Value at Risk (VaR), Responsive VaR, and backtesting techniques. c. Interpret and evaluate regulatory frameworks like Basel norms and its guidelines for capital adequacy and systemic risk control. d. Develop risk mitigation strategies using derivatives, including hedging techniques and options Greeks, to manage exposure effectively. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division
topics: Introduction to financial risk; Market, Credit, Liquidity, Operational, Interest Rate, Business, Bankruptcy, Default, Settlement and Systemic Risk; Enterprise Risk; Risk–Return Trade-off; Asset Pricing Models (CAPM, Multifactor Models including Fama–French Models).

Functions and workings of financial institutions: banks, hedge funds, mutual funds etc. Risk management practices in FIs. Basel Accord (Basel-I, II, III), Basel III capital structure (CET1, AT1 and Tier II Capital), Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR), Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB), Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), leverage ratio, Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Pillar I, Pillar II and Pillar III requirements, Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP), stress testing and scenario analysis, market-risk reforms under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), and the role of Basel regulations in strengthening the resilience and stability of the global financial system.

Probability distributions; Statistical concepts for risk modelling; Time-series properties of financial returns; Stochastic Processes; Geometric Brownian Motion; Itô's Lemma; Black–Scholes–Merton Model; Numerical methods and interpolation techniques; L17-27 Risk modeling – Value at risk, C-VaR, Marginal VaR, Component VaR, Options VaR, Fixed income VaR, Credit VaR, scenarios analysis and stress testing, back testing.

Risk management using option Greeks, implied volatility, volatility smile, volatility surface, volatility modeling, VIX modeling and application. L36-40 Risk management of fixed income securities. (Optional)

This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. about: The course is planned to give a comprehensive working knowledge of Advertising and Marketing communication and how they inter-relate. It offers modules, case studies and do-it your own assignment opportunities. The main feature of the course is that it is constantly evolving, keeping itself relevant to the needs of the advertising industry. Today’s student is expected to understand all the major marketing functions: advertising, its process, integrated marketing communication involving across multimedia: podcast/podcasts, newspaper, magazine, television, and via Internet. It aims to enable the students to familiarize the advertising communication process and how it works in relation to market and the consumers. a. To introduce advertising with IMC perspectives b. To expose the students to the traditional and digital media for advertising e. To familiarize the students about global advertising and promotion scenario along with rural marketing f. To sensitize them about various ethical issues when planning and implementing advertising and promotional programs g. To underscore the implications of AI within advertising realm a. title: Introductory Psychology
about: Psychology as a science, Perception, its nature, determinants, and measurement; Biological bases of behaviour; Consciousness, Motivation, and Emotion; Learning and behaviour modification; Memory and forgetting; Thought processes, Problemsolving, and Creative thinking; Individual differences—Intelligence, Gender, Personality, Stress, and Coping; Social thought and Social Behaviour; with an emphasis on psychological assessment, behavioural data, research analytics, and evidence-based decision-making. To develop a conceptual framework for understanding the human behaviour; relevance of psychology in daily life and its application in social, educational, industrial, personal and other spheres. Explain the major concepts, theories, and principles of psychology, including the biological, cognitive, emotional, developmental, personality, and social foundations of human behaviour. Apply psychological principles to analyse everyday individual and social behaviour, decision-making, learning, motivation, stress, and interpersonal interactions. Compare and critically evaluate major psychological perspectives, theories, and empirical evidence to explain human thought, emotion, and behaviour. Demonstrate an understanding of psychological research methods, ethical principles, basic research design, and the interpretation of psychological data. Evaluate individual differences in perception, intelligence, personality, emotion, and behaviour using evidence-based psychological concepts and appropriate assessment approaches. Integrate psychological knowledge to promote self-awareness, effective communication, well-being, problem-solving, and responsible decision-making in academic, professional, and social contexts.

title: Effective Public Speaking
about: Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; NonVerbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and deliveringEffective Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion and Job Interviews The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy, audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. Classroom Methodology The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice-oriented and develops speaking skills through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and presentation tasks. Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.
topics: Using Body and Voice to Communicate

title: Marxian Thought
about: This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures. Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without fundamentally exploitative structures. Selections from these books and viewing material will be used based on the requirements of the class. o A Reader’s Guide to Marx’s Capital - Joseph Choonara o Chapters from Yanis Varoufakis o Selected Readings from Ha-Joon Chang Film Clippings for Class Discussion: Mandi, Yashowardhan Mishra (2019); Rang de Basanti (2006); Bread and Roses, Ken Loach (2000); The Wind that Shakes the Barley, Ken Loach (2006); Nae Pasaran, Felipe Bustos Sierra (2018) 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division

title: TECHNIQUES IN SOCIAL RESEARCH
about: Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics). This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data. Explain the philosophical foundations, paradigms, and methodological approaches of social research, and distinguish between qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research designs. Design ethically sound social research studies by formulating research problems, conducting literature reviews, selecting appropriate research designs, sampling strategies, and data collection methods. Apply principles of measurement, reliability, validity, scale development, and sampling to develop rigorous research instruments for social science investigations. Analyze quantitative and qualitative data using appropriate statistical and qualitative analysis techniques, including the use of software such as SPSS, Jamovi, and NVivo. Evaluate and interpret findings from diverse research methodologies, including experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, content analysis, and secondary data research, to draw evidence-based conclusions. Prepare and communicate research reports that demonstrate ethical research practices, critical interpretation of findings, and effective use of research analytics and visualization tools for scholarly dissemination.

title: Cross Cultural Skills
about: Providing insights into intercultural communication with powerful and deeply held views from multiple cultures. Familiarizing the students how to undertake that critical self-reflection which may lead to better appreciation of the cultural diversity possessed by communities worldwide. Bringing into the discussions, the experiences of intercultural communication, knowledge of the field of communication studies and mass communication, and perceptions of intercultural communication as a woman and as men from diverse ethnic, racial and cultural backgrounds. Using AI to enhance cross-cultural understanding, communication, and adaptation through interactive learning and real-world simulations. Understand cross-cultural communication and its different dimensions based on national cultures, as propounded by Geert Hofstede and Edward T. Develop sensitivity to cultural variations in thinking, feeling, and behaving and adapting the same for cross-cultural communication effectiveness. Learn management and interpersonal skills to reckon, predict, and leverage cultural differences. Develop an appreciation for the global mindset vis-à-vis Indian cultural identity. Know more about diverse national cultures and countries from class projects and presentations. title: Introductory Philosophy
about: An overview of major philosophical traditions from the Western and Indian worlds. The course traces the nature and purpose of philosophy from classical Greek thought through modern rationalism, empiricism, and existentialism before turning to the classical Indian schools. A critical survey of major Western and Indian philosophical viewpoints, from antiquity to contemporary thought. The course aims to equip students with the tools to critically evaluate philosophical arguments and to appreciate their relevance to questions of knowledge, ethics, and selfhood in human life. Course Learning Objectives Upon completion of the course students will have An understanding of the various philosophical schools of Indian and Western traditions. A critical and comparative grasp of the philosophical viewpoints & debates. An ability to build theoretical constructions and extend philosophical thinking to other disciplines. An ability to practice the habit of thinking rationally and critically in leading an ethical and meaningful life

title: SCIENCE FICTION
about: Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias, dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist, postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal; and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling. Introduce students to science fiction as a literary mode that critiques technological and social change. Explore how science fiction engages with questions of environment and the posthuman through narrative. Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination. Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of science and cultural studies.
topics: STORY What is Science Fiction? Definitions; sense of wonder; science vs. imagination; SF’s Golden Age. Arthur C. Clarke (The Nine Billion Names of God)
STORY Environmental collapse; ethics of survival; concept of utopia and dystopia. Ray Bradbury (There Will Come Soft Rains)
MOVIE Anime and Apocalypse; nuclear anxiety; technology and the city. Screening & discussion: Akira (1988)
STORY Feminist SF; reproduction and body politics; invisibility and gendered futures. Octavia Butler (Bloodchild)
STORY Science, empire, urban ecologies and local imaginaries. Vandana Singh (Delhi), Nnedi Okorafor (Spider the Artist)
Futurity and cultural resistance. Comparative analysis: Singh, Okorafor
MOVIE Metaphysical SF; memory, grief, and the alien. Tarkovsky’s Solaris (screening & discussion)
STORY AI and autonomy; consciousness and ethics; digital life as species-being. Ted Chiang (The Lifecycle of Software Objects)
MOVIE Human vs. alien communication. Arrival (screening & discussion)

title: Human Resource Development
about: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources with special reference to its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement, and societal development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately productivity) of the employees can be enhanced. To develop a conceptual framework for understanding human behavior in organizations and develop human capital (manpower) in various sectors and spheres of the world of work. The course would be very beneficial for students trying to understand the management functions of one very significant department of any organization. To get a superficial idea about various training/skill development exercises and processes encompassing such activities.

title: SRIMAD BHAGAVAD GITA
about: This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhaktiyoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge. Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship (abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail. Course Learning Objectives Explain the principal philosophical concepts of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, including isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala, and karma, and the relationship among them. Differentiate and analyse the major paths of yoga—karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, dhyana-yoga, and bhakti-yoga—along with their purpose and practical significance. Apply the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita to improve time management, stress management, concentration, emotional balance, self-discipline, decision-making, and overall well-being in academic and personal life. _ BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY & SCIENCE, PILANI PILANI CAMPUS AUGS/AGSR DIVISIONS
topics: What is Bhagavad-gita; the five subject matters of Bhagavad-gita
Setting the scene; infallible Vedic knowledge-four defects, ways of gaining knowledge; sanatana dharma

Arjuna’s dilemmas and doubts; perplexities of life in this world: birth, death, disease and old age, three-fold miseries; material relationships: temporary, cause misery; the only solution: spiritual relationship
Absolute necessity of spiritual relationship with a bona fide spiritual master/teacher; qualifications of a spiritual master; check and balance through Guru, sadhu and sastra
Ascending knowledge vs. descending knowledge; importance of hearing; process of hearing
What is soul? Proof of existence of soul, its nature and individuality; the doctrine of ‘life comes from life’; activities in knowledge of the science of soul
Cause of suffering in this world; constitutional position of living entity
Knowing the Supreme personality of Godhead; Understanding both God’s material and spiritual energies, and the supreme controller; understanding the position of God, His expansions and living entities
Lord’s descent: His love, purpose and mission; Paramatma: our ever well-wishing best friend
Inconceivable nature of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, His qualities and pastimes; cultivating spiritual relationship being the only way to understand Him.
Is God personal or impersonal? Three aspects of the Absolute Truth; path of personalism vs. path of impersonalism
Demigod worship: universal administration; demigods and their relationship with God; right way to approach demigods
What is yoga? Types of yoga – dhyana, karma, jnana, bhakti; limitation of asthanga yoga in kali yuga; gradual and direct method - bhakti yoga; pure devotional service; the topmost yoga system

Three modes of material nature: conditioning of the living entity; characteristics of goodness, passion and ignorance; how the modes bind us; free will and destiny; working for God and working for maya; Supreme Lord is transcendental to modes; liberation from three modes

Why bad things happen to good people? Law of karma: good karma, bad karma and akarma; how to become free from karma and rebirth; karma kanda: flowery language of Vedas; karma yoga and its importance; contemporary relevance of karma yoga; sakama and nishkama karma yoga
Time (kala) and its influence; impact of this understanding on our heart (“nimita matram bhava savya sachin”)
Four types of people who surrender to God; four types of people who don’t surrender to God; difference between transcendental and demoniac qualities; returning to our divine nature
Qualities which endear one to God; Krishna’s concluding instructions; Arjuna’s understanding and realizations
Sanjaya’s realizations; way to be victorious.

title: Professional Ethics
about: An introduction to the ethical concepts, theories, and codes that govern professional life. The course traces the foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management, education, engineering, and computing. This course provides a formal acquaintance with the concepts and frameworks of ethics; recognize the codes of ethics relevant to the experience of being a professional and develops an understanding of the ethical issues relating to professions generally, and to business, management, education, engineering, and computing in particular. Through the analysis of real-time case studies, students learn to appreciate the role of moral reasoning in issues of professional life. Upon completion of the course students will have An understanding of the core concepts of ethics, the profession, and professional ethics, and their specific application across business, management, education, engineering, and computing. A critical and comparative grasp of competing ethical theories and professional viewpoints such as rulefollowing versus professional judgment. An ability to apply ethical theories and frameworks to real, contested professional dilemmas, extending this reasoning across multiple professional domains rather than any single one. An ability to practice the habit of sound ethical judgment and professional responsibility in one's own future career and conduct.

title: INTERNATIONALRELATIONS
about:  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health RegimePandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States. International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.
topics: Why study International Relations? The context of its emergence as a discipline (1-3)
Evolution of the Contemporary State System and Sovereignty; World Wars; League of Nations and United Nations Organizations; Cold War and Fall of USSR (7-11)
Security in IR: Nuclear Deterrence; Terrorism and Counterterrorism; Non- traditional Threats and Wars (27-30)
Human Rights; Climate Change and Pandemic in IR (31-33)

title: ECOCRITICISM
about: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the wellbeing of our planet. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts.

title: Electrical Machines
about: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machinesuniversal motors, Induction generators. Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts. The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
about: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.
topics: Brief history, recent trends and crystal lattices
Semiconductor models Charge carriers, effective mass.
Statistics of donors and acceptors, Space charge neutrality.
Optical absorption, excess carrier, Quasi- Fermi level

MOS structure, MOS Transistors, I-V characteristics and secondary effects
BJT operations, terminal current, Gummel plot, small-signal model, charge control model
Photodiodes, Solar cells, and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and their advanced version

title: Linear Algebra and its Applications
about: Quick review of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations, Basis and Dimension, rank-nullity theorem, change of basis; Inner product spaces, Cauchy Schwarz's inequality, GramSchmidt orthonormalization, QR decomposition, Discrete Fourier Transform, and their applications, Spectral Theorem, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, Decomposition theorem, and Jordan canonical forms, applications of SVD in Principal Component Analysis, use of SVD in low-rank approximations and to find least-squares solutions. Linear algebra has applications in pure and applied mathematics, computer science, economics, engineering, mathematical biology, operation research, physics, and statistics. Linear algebra and matrix methods are also important for data analysis. Linear Algebra and its applications typically aim to equip students with a solid understanding of fundamental concepts in linear algebra and the ability to apply these concepts to the above fields. After completion of this course students should be able to : Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to construct orthonormal bases in inner product spaces. Utilize Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities to prove geometric boundaries and inner product behaviors. Factor a matrix into orthogonal and upper triangular components for stable numerical computations. Implement the Spectral Theorem and structural decomposition theorems Formulate and compute optimal least-squares solutions for linear models using pseudoinverses derived from SVD. Apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to execute Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on high-dimensional datasets.

Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable. about: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs. title: Elementary Real Analysis
about: Countable and uncountable sets, Real numbers and their properties, Sequence of real numbers, Continuous functions of real variable, Metric space, Compact set, Connected set, Completeness, Continuous function on a metric space, Riemann integration, Sequence and series of functions. This course aims to discuss several properties of real numbers and functions of real variables. The notions of metric spaces will be introduced and a few concepts in analysis, such as continuity, the convergence of sequences, the convergence of sequences and series of functions, will be discussed. We will also discuss the rigorous theory of Riemann integration. Students will also learn to read and write rigorous proofs so that they can communicate mathematical ideas effectively. This course is also a basic course to build background for other advanced courses in mathematics. Students will learn about real numbers and their elementary properties, sequences of real numbers, and the generalization of distance to abstract sets. Students will be introduced to the notion of convergence of series and sequence of functions. Students will study the rigorous theory of integration.

title: Multivariable Calculus
about: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion. about: Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques. title: Ordinary Differential Equations
about: Existence and uniqueness theorems; properties of linear systems; behavior of solutions of nth order equations; asymptotic behavior of linear systems; stability of linear and weakly nonlinear systems; conditions for boundedness and the number of zeros of the nontrivial solutions of second order equations; stability by Lyapunov's direct method; autonomous and non-autonomous systems. Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life. title: Combinatorial Mathematics
about: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach. Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting. The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. At the end of the course, student will be aware of many existing methods used to solve counting problems and when these methods are applicable.

title: Applied Statistical Methods
about: Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statistical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, realizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinterpretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference, analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R. This 4th level course is designed with a two-fold purpose. First, it will provide an exposure to various theoretical univariate/multivariate methods and their practical applications.
