title: Multivariable Calculus
about: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs. Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.  CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.  CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.  CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.  CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.  CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.  CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems.

about: The subject matter in this course covers the applications of thermodynamics. This course is designed to acquaint the students with the thermodynamics of power generating and power absorbing machines. The course discusses gas and vapour power cycles, boilers, combined cycle power generation, vapour compression and absorption refrigeration cycles, gas mixtures, psychrometry, and air-conditioning, building cooling/heating load estimation.

title: Engines, Motors, and Mobility
about: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles. This course has been designed to make the students familiar with internal combustion engines and electric and hybrid electric power trains.

title: Energy Storage Technologies
about: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems. The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior. T.B. 1: Robert A. Huggins, Energy Storage: Fundamentals, Materials and Applications, Springer, 2nd Edition, 2016. T.B. 2: Reddy, Linden’s Handbook of Batteries, McGraw-Hill Education, 3rd Edition, 2011. R.B. 1: Luisa F. Cabeza, Advances in Thermal Energy Storage Systems: Methods and Applications, Elsevier Science & Technology, ProQuest Ebook Central, 2014. title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
about: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices. The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the microand nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains. text Introduction to 1-2 Introduction to microfluidics What is microfluidics, importance and T1, Ch1, Microfluidics applications, Challenges, R1 Ch1 Commercial activities 3-4 Scaling in microfluidics Physics of miniaturization, Scaling T1, Ch1, laws R1 Ch1, R2 Ch1 5-6 Intermolecular forces, States of Governing equations and matter, Continuum assumption, T1, Ch2, Constitutive relations Governing equations, Constitutive R1 Ch2 relations. Micro-scale fluid 7-13 Low Re flows, Slip theory, Entrance T1, Ch2, mechanics and effects, Stokes drag on a sphere, Exact R1 Ch3, Micro scale flows and solutions, Couette flow, Poiseuille pressure driven R2 Ch2, pressure driven microflows flow, microflows class

title: Continuum Mechanics
about: Introduction to tensors, tensor algebra and tensor calculus. Kinematics of deformation (displacement, velocity, deformation gradient, material and spatial field descriptions, description of local deformation, linearized kinematics, kinematic rates), left & right Cauchy-Green deformation tensor, Cauchy-Lagrangian strain tensor. Traction and stress (first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, second PiolaKirchhoff stress, Biot stress etc). Mechanical conservation and balance laws (conservation of mass, conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, conservation of energy, work done by stresses and the principle of virtual work, BVP, IVP, calculus of variation). Constitutive relations (constraints on constitutive relations, frame indifference, objectivity, material symmetry, constitutive models for linearly elastic, hyperelastic solids and fluid flows). This course will provide an introduction to continuum mechanics. It aims to develop in students the foundational mathematical rigor needed to understand advanced topics in solid and fluid mechanics.

title: SMART MATERIALS
about: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electroand magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structuralhealth monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices. This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulusresponsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further projectand researchoriented work in smart materials and structures. CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

about: Principles, thermodynamic analysis, load estimates and design of various refrigeration and air conditioning systems for comfort and industrial applications. title: Mechanism and Robotics
about: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain.
topics: History and evolution of robotics; Difference between mechanisms, machines, and robots; Classification of robots (industrial, service, humanoid, mobile); Applications in manufacturing, healthcare, defense, and space
Basic terminology (links, joints, kinematic pairs); Degrees of freedom (DOF) and mobility; Gruebler’s equation; Planar vs. spatial mechanisms; Four-bar linkages and coupler curves

Forward kinematics and transformation matrices; Denavit–Hartenberg (D-H) parameters (standard & modified); Frame assignment rules; Inverse kinematics (analytical & numerical methods); Workspace analysis and redundancy
Differential motion and velocity propagation; Jacobian matrix derivation for serial robots; Manipulability and velocity ellipsoids; Singularities and their impact on control
Newton-Euler and Lagrangian formulations; Forward and inverse dynamics problems; Dynamic modeling of manipulators; Payload capacity, torque requirements, and force analysis
control systems; Joint space (PID) control strategies; Task space control (computed torque, adaptive control); Hybrid position- force control
Mobile robot kinematics and navigation; Path and trajectory planning (C- space, PRM, RRT); Robot vision (camera calibration, image processing); AI and machine learning integration in robotics
Industrial robot configurations (SCARA, Cartesian, articulated); Robot programming methods (teach pendant & offline); End-effectors and grippers design; Case studies of robotic automation in industry
Collaborative robots (cobots) and human-robot interaction; Soft robotics and bio-inspired robots; Swarm robotics; Course review and student project presentations

title: Finite Element Method
about: Fundamental concepts, matrix algebra and gaussian elimination, one-dimensional problems, trusses, two-dimensional problems using constant strain triangles, axisymmetric solids subjected to axisymmetric loading, two-dimensional isoparametric elements and numerical integration, beams and frames, three-dimensional problems in stress analysis, scalar field problems, dynamic considerations, pre-processing and post processing. The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathematical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built. CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz method. CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer. CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid mechanics and heat transfer.

FE modelling of Beams and Frames

title: Industrial Robotics and Controls
about: This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing environments. This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis, and operation of industrial robotic manipulators. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-andplace, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC GRADUATE STUDIES AND RESEARCH DIVISION (T1) Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control — John J. title: Moulding Methods for Electronic Components
about: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plasticmoulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components. Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry. This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry, as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies. CO No. Course Outcome CO1 Develop an understanding of the moulding processes and testing techniques involved in the fabrication of plastic components in the electronics industry. CO2 Selection of appropriate materials for the electronic industry. CO3 Design and fabricate different plastic components using moulding processes. CO4 Acquire basic design skills related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould. CO5 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical electronic component fabrication problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.
topics: L (1-2): Introduction to Electronic Components Manufacturing: Overview of the electronic manufacturing industry, types of electronic components manufactured, importance of encapsulation and moulding in electronic components, historical evolution, and trends in electronic moulding, role of mould in protecting and enhancing performance.

L (3-5): Material selection and properties: different metallic, polymeric, ceramic, and composite materials used in the electronics industry. Material Selection Criteria: material properties, including electrical properties, thermal stability, mechanical properties, and environmental resistance. Polymer material characterization and testing.

L (6-20): Plastic Moulding Techniques: Principles, process fundamentals, tooling involved, material selection, and process parameters for different processes, including injection moulding, compression moulding, transfer moulding, blow moulding, pressure casting, and die casting. Case study.

L (21-35): Design of Moulds: Design aspects of moulds used for plastic component fabrication, Injection Mould Design: different elements, cooling system, ejection system. Design of blow mould, compression mould, and transfer mould. Case study.

L (35-40): Polymer-based Additive Manufacturing: Introduction, classification, advantages, disadvantages, and applications. Different processes, including Vat photo Polymerization, powder bed fusion, material jetting, material extrusion, and binder jetting: principle, equipment, process, materials, and post- processing.

title: Computer Aided Design & Additive Manufacturing
about: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course introduces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products. The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric modelling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques. It enables students to apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products. Understand the mathematical and computational foundations of parametric geometric modelling; Construct and interpret curves, surfaces, solids, assemblies, and product-data representations; Apply ASME Y14.5 concepts to communicate functional dimensional and geometric requirements; Formulate and interpret generative-design and topology-optimization problems; 1 Understand additive-manufacturing processes, materials, preprocessing, process parameters, post-processing, and safety; and Integrate CAD, GD&T, optimization, and additive manufacturing in a coherent digital product-development workflow.

title: Theory of Elasticity & Plasticity
about: The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow, Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes. Course Level Objectives: The course is for higher degree students to prepare them in applying the theory on some problems of practical and design interest. The students will be able to appreciate underlying meaning of material and structural behavior under complex loading conditions. Students are also encouraged to do assignments using the ANSYS/ABAQUS package to solve problems of elasticity and plasticity to compare the analytical solutions. CO1: Understand the concept of stress and strain in situations where large deformations are involved. CO2: Appreciate the governing differential equations that describe a general boundary value problem in elasticity. CO3: Solve the general elasticity boundary value problems with various boundary conditions using methods of complex variable techniques CO4: Appreciate the concept of yielding and yield criteria. Yield surface and normality rule, associated flow rule

Torsion in straight bars of non-circular cross sections, Hollow sections, Plastic theory of torsion: Stresses beyond elastic limit
Physics of Plasticity, Steady state problems in plane strain

Constitutive relations, Problems contained plastic deformation, True stress-strain curve, strain rate effects, idealization, Yield criteria, plastic stress-strain relations, Symmetrical extrusion, Unsymmetrical extrusion, multi-hole extrusion, Sheet drawing, Cold rolling, mechanics of hot rolling

title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
about: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices. The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the microand nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains. title: SMART MATERIALS
about: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electroand magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structuralhealth monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices. This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulusresponsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further projectand researchoriented work in smart materials and structures. CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

about: Basic concepts of probability and probability distribution, Standard probability distribution, Sampling and Sampling Distributions, Confidence intervals, testing significance, Statistical tolerance, Various types of control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into production process. This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their never-ending quest for quality.

title: ADVANCED VLSI DESIGN
about: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips. The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system. Students will develop an understanding of common design and timing issues/challenges in digital systems. They will be introduced to high-speed/low-power circuit logic/ power minimization techniques, as well as wiring models used in digital systems. Additionally, they will learn about the clock system design and various noise sources that can interfere with these systems.
topics: General Introduction- digital system, data rate, pin count, serial/ parallel communication, eye diagram
Signal encoding, and signaling modes, voltage/ current Input/output drivers (with low power constraint) for C, and LRC loads
Timing issues in synchronous VLSI systems. Asynchronous system design
Wire design models in the nanometer region- lumped, distributed, transmission line, termination
High-performance / low-power circuit logic, delay/ power minimization using logical effort
Clock signals distribution and clock generation, clock drivers, Digital phase locked loop, digital delay locked loop, synchronizer - design and meta-stability issues

title: Advanced VLSI Architectures
about: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures. The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors a. Explain the advantages of CORDIC in hardware implementation, especially in terms of multiplier-less architecture, low power, and area efficiency. b. Analyze the design principles of advanced VLSI processor architectures and their microarchitectural implementation strategies for high-performance computing systems. c. Evaluate various memory hierarchy designs and optimizations, including their microarchitectural aspects, in the context of different processor types. d. Apply concepts of parallelism—such as instruction-level, data-level, thread-level, and task-level parallelism—to optimize system performance. e. Design architectural solutions using specialized processing units such as SIMD processors, vector processors, multimedia processors, GPUs, multi-core systems, and domain-specific accelerators. f. Explore contemporary research trends and emerging technologies in VLSI processor and memory system architecture to identify potential areas for innovation.
topics: Fundamentals of Quantitative Design and Analysis

Implement of Biasing Circuits and Optical/Wireline Receiver Transmitter circuits. Pilani Campus A UGSD/AGSRD Division e. Understand and Apply analog layout methodologies, matching principles, and noise-aware design techniques. f. title: Digital VLSI Design
about: We will study the fundamental structures of VLSI Systems at the lowest levels of system abstraction, namely those associated with the direct application of VLSI devices to particular problems of interest. The broad topics of coverage includes Principles of operations of CMOS transistors used as a digital switch and various other topologies used in Digital VLSI Design, Logic implementation strategies and performance characterization of the VLSI circuits, Low Power Design, different clocking strategies, symbolic layout systems, CMOS subsystems design and Memory modules. The objective of this course is to understand the need and importance of digital VLSI design in CMOS integrated circuits. To understand different design principles used in the design of Digital VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS with emphasis on low power and high performance.

title: AUTOMATION AND CONTROL
about: This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt, due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems. Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies, combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly enhanced by the application of mechatronics. This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation systems.

title: Lean Manufacturing
about: small lot production, setup time reduction, maintaining and improving equipment, pull production systems, focused factories and group technologies, work cells and cellular manufacturing, standard operations, quality of design, systems for eliminating defects, simplified production planning and control systems: scheduling for smooth flow, synchronizing and balancing process, planning and control in pull production, beyond the production systems: managing the supply chain, activity based costing, performance measurement. In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from pricecutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of longterm philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the Toyota way

title: Marketing
about: This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions. On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course. Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment.
topics: Building Customer satisfaction, Value and retention
Positioning and differentiating the market offering

title: Managing People & Organization
about: individual, group, and organizational systems. It examines variables and key concepts related to individual attitudes, motivation, and leadership, along with group dynamics, organizational structure, and change management, while also covering the strategic role of HRM in attracting, developing, motivating, and retaining talent through recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, compensation, and talent management. In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover, management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and developed.  CLO1. Comprehend the fundamental concepts in organizational behavior and human resource management and the tight coupling between them  CLO2. title: Statistics & Basic Econometrics
about: Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course. This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R. Apply statistical and econometric models to estimate relevant business parameters, predict economic outcomes, and test hypotheses using quantitative data. Understand the fundamental assumptions underlying the classical linear regression model and identify and address potential violations, such as autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity. Develop and sustain a foundational knowledge of econometrics that will serve as a basis for further study in business analytics and advanced statistical methodologies.

title: Data Management & Warehousing (DMW)
about: This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights from databases through data analytics powered by SQL. The course covers various Database Management and Data Warehousing concepts and enhances learning effectiveness through developing scripting skills. It aims to provide students with the necessary knowledge and skills to understand the data infrastructure underpinning business intelligence and analytics. Students undertaking this course should be able to appreciate the complexities involved in Database management and be prepared to solve the issues a business analyst faces.  Understand the database environment and the complete development process, including requirements gathering, design, and implementation.  Model data using Entity-Relationship diagrams and design logical and physical relational databases.  Write effective SQL queries to manage and manipulate data within relational databases.  Explain the architecture of database applications, foundations of data warehousing, and principles of data quality and integration.  Explore the role of databases in Big Data analytics and understand essential tasks in database administration.
topics: Database Design Using the E-R Model
Preparing a relational model using logical database design

title: Deep Learning for Business
about: This course offers an introduction to deep learning and its practical relevance in business contexts. It covers foundational concepts such as neural networks, linear and logistic regression using neural architectures, deep neural networks, hyperparameter tuning, and advanced models like CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs, GANs, and deep reinforcement learning. The course blends theoretical understanding with hands-on applications to solve real-world business problems. It also highlights the challenges and limitations of deep learning methods in practice. The course aims to equip students with foundational and practical knowledge of deep learning algorithms and their applications in solving business challenges. The a. Understanding core deep learning architectures and techniques b. Translating business problems into machine learning tasks c. Developing, training, and tuning deep learning models using appropriate tools d. Applying deep learning to solve business challenges e. Utilizing TensorFlow and Keras libraries on Google Colab to implement and explore deep learning algorithms f. Recognizing the limitations, ethical concerns, and interpretability issues of deep models in business decision-making g. Engaging in a group-based project, where students apply deep learning techniques to some realworld business problems a. Understand the fundamental principles of neural networks and deep learning algorithms, including their relevance to solving business problems. b. Develop and train deep neural networks, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), using TensorFlow and Keras on Google Colab. c. Implement and fine-tune models through effective hyperparameter optimization strategies. d. Use deep learning techniques to address business use cases. e. Conduct group projects that involve problem formulation, data preparation, model development, and presentation of results for real-world business problems. f. Assess the challenges, limitations, and ethical implications of deploying deep learning models in business problems. g. Communicate technical outcomes and business insights from deep learning models to both technical and non-technical stakeholders. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division

title: PRESCRIPTIVE ANALYTICS WITH MATHEMATICAL
about: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of postmortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHONOLOGY AND SCIENCE, PILANI Pilani Campus Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution) based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints. Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved. a. Students will be able to formulate prescriptive analytics real-life problems and use their applications. b. Students will learn the basics of Linear Programming, Transportation and Assignment problems, Integer Programming, Waiting Line Problems, Simulation modeling, and Goal Programming c. Students will be able to formulate real-life large-sized problems in Lingo software and solve them. They will also learn how to interpret Lingo results and apply them to real-world decisionmaking for prescriptive analytics problems.
topics: (I) (i) Operations Research Approach to Problem Solving
Linear Programming (LP): Model Formulation and Graphical Solution
(ii) Linear Programming: Computer Solution and Sensitivity Analysis
Solving Linear Programming (OR) Problems in Lingo
(III) (i) Waiting Lines and Queuing Theory Models
Some Advanced Applications of Prescriptive Analytics

title: Marketing Research & Metrics
about: All organizations need to research their markets periodically and employ various elements of marketing research process viz. problem definition, development of an approach to the problem, research design formulation, fieldwork & data collection, data preparation & analysis and finally report preparation and presentation. The emphasis of the course is proportionately focused on foundational concepts, methodology & techniques, and marketing research applications. A number of cases will be assigned for discussion in the class. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” and a project assignment in this course characterizes this orientation. To impart necessary foundational concepts, methodologies and tools/techniques for role of a market researcher. That role envisages generation of actionable, reliable and accurate information to identify various marketing problems viz. demand forecasting, segmentation, targeting, positioning, new product development etc. and find their effective solutions.

title: Financial Modelling and Valuation
about: A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division knowledge of financial analysis and discover how companies produce and quantify value for their investors. This is a fairly challenging and ambitious course by design. We will use case studies and problem-solving techniques because the course objectives are grounded on the practical application of academic ideas. There will be lectures and discussions throughout class time. The readings will be integrated into the lectures' analytic principles, which will provide a helpful framework for a deeper comprehension of the instances. Please keep in mind that the goal of a valuation exercise is to use a series of techniques and logical steps that represent the complexity of the situation, not to get it "precise." title: People Analytics
about: There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises, questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test comprehension of the theory and readings. People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability.  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division  The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision making.  The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.  Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).  Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.  Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make data driven decision making.  Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results.

However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability.  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division  The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision making.  The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.  Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).  Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.  Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make data driven decision making.  Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results.

about: Basic techniques of pharmaceutical analysis, data handling and analysis, sources of error in analysis. title: PHARMACEUTICAL FORMULATIONS II
about: Physical, chemical, and biopharmaceutical considerations in formulations, absorption, distribution, and elimination of drugs; pharmaceutical additives; formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of solid dosage forms, semi-solid dosage forms, liquids dosage forms, and sterile preparations including parenteral suspensions, emulsions, depot formulations; microencapsulation and controlled release formulations; targeted drug delivery systems; multi-unit particulate systems; transdermal, gastroretentive, and nasopulmonary drug delivery systems; aerosol products and packaging. It is a course intended to give students insight into the problems involved in making drug dosage forms. It brings together the various sciences involved in developing pharmaceutical product formulations and evaluating their quality. The laboratory component involves some fundamental exercises in the evolution of products such as tablets, ointments, solutions, parenteral products, sustained-action medications, etc. It also imparts knowledge of newer dosage forms. Explain the principles of preformulation, formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of conventional pharmaceutical dosage forms, including solid, liquid, semi-solid, and sterile preparations. Apply pharmaceutical formulation principles and standard manufacturing techniques to prepare and evaluate conventional and modified-release dosage forms, while adhering to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and quality requirements. Compare and evaluate the design, advantages, limitations, and pharmaceutical applications of novel drug delivery systems, including controlled-release, targeted, transdermal, gastroretentive, multiparticulate, nasopulmonary, and aerosol dosage forms.

Formulation of different dosage forms: Tablets, liquids, semisolids, and injectables

title: Immunopharmacology
about: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development.
topics: Immunodeficiency diseases, allergy and hypersensitivity reactions

title: Modern Pharmaceutical Analytical Techniques
about: This course is a laboratory oriented course and covers various analytical aspects like principles of sample preparation, method development for analysis and characterization of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) and formulations, using techniques such as High Performance Liquid chromatography (HPLC), biochromatography, size exclusion, affinity, chiral, fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC). Characterization of nanopharmaceutcials using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) techniques. 1H and 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in structural characterization, Mass Spectrometry and its applications, Elemental analysis, Optical, chiro-optical techniques in structure elucidation. The course is aimed at exposing the students to modern analytical techniques in relevance to pharmaceutical industries. Training with respect to the handling and operation of sophisticated instruments, interpretation of results obtained for the characterization of molecules, their qualitative and quantitative evaluation are emphasized. Handling of analytical instruments for performing qualitative and quantitative analyses of drugs. Design and development of suitable analytical methods for drugs based on their physico-chemical characters meeting the standard requirements. Ability to interpret the analytical graphs and spectra for drug identification, characterization, evaluation and decision making.
topics: Introduction to Modern Pharmaceutical Analytical techniques.

title: Computer Aided Drug Design
about: 3D structure and function of bio-molecules; targets of drugs and design principles; molecular modeling methodologies; quantitative structure-activity relationships; chemical compound databases and search tools; interactive graphics in drug design; molecular surfaces and algorithm of automated docking of drugs into receptor sites; receptor mapping; introduction to molecular modeling and docking software. To develop an appreciation of interand intramolecular energies and forces. To introduce the techniques of computational chemistry and to demonstrate their application to the design of drugs. title: Advanced Physical Pharmaceutics
about: Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like, pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study, specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in-vitro in-vivo correlation (IVIVC), polymer science, etc. Prior to the development of any dosage form with a new or old drug candidate, it is essential that certain fundamental physical and chemical properties of the drug molecule and other derived properties of the drug are determined. This information dictates possible approaches in formulation development. The aim of this course is to make the students understand those physicochemical principles which must be applied in the formulation and development of an efficacious dosage form, so that required duration and intensity of effect can be ensured at the intended site of action. R3: ICH Q guidelines -http://www.ich.org/fileadmin/Public_Web_Site/ICH_Products/ Guidelines/Quality R 4: Sanford Bolton, Charles Bon, Pharmaceutical Statistics, Informa Healthcare, 5th Edition, 2010.

title: CLINICAL RESEARCH
about: Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial managementcoordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report preparation for various submissions. There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical, biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills required to design, monitor, and manage clinical trials. Courses include the drug development process; regulations, guidelines, and standards; research methodology and biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring, and documentation; and project management. title: Pharmacokinetics & Clinical Pharmacy
about: Introduction to pharmacokinetic modeling of drugs; Compartmental modeling including one compartmental and two compartmental models; Non-compartmental analysis (NCA); Bioequivalence and comparative bioavailability studies; Pharmacokinetic Pharmacodynamic modeling techniques, determination of order of absorption and absorption rate constant by Wagner-Nelson method; non-linear pharmacokinetics; Pharmacokinetic drug interactions; multi-dose pharmacokinetics of drugs following one compartmental model; Design of multi-dose regimen; Dosage regimen adjustment in renal impairment; Application of the pharmacokinetic principles for better therapeutic outcomes The course imparts knowledge of pharmacokinetics, its application, pharmacokinetic studies, mathematical modeling, and experimental design. This will help students to gain knowledge in a very important area of pharmacy. Practicals are designed to expose students to pharmacokinetic studies.
topics: Pharmacokinetics (ADME) studies after different routes of administration and Compartment Models
Multiple Dosing Studies and Non Compartment Analysis
Bioavailability, Bioequivalence studies, physiological and pharmacokinetic models
Pharmacokinetic parameters in hepatic and renal impairment, Q.S.Pk.R, Experimental techniques in pharmacokinetics

title: Pharmaceutical Biotechnology
about: The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular biology, molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bioinformatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. title: Pharmaceutical Administration & Management (PAM)
about: This course introduces students to various organizational aspects, focusing on pharmaceutical management. Topics include technology innovation, drug planning, strategy, project execution, product development, production, scale-up, marketing, IPR, HR, industrial relations, documentation, R&D, and ethics. The objective of the course is to help students understand new drug and product considerations and planning; strategic considerations; project implementation; product development; production management & scale-up; marketing strategy; human resources development; ethical issues; and R&D management. Explain the principles of pharmaceutical product innovation, new drug and product planning, strategic decision-making, project implementation, and product development processes in the pharmaceutical industry. Apply the concepts of production management, scale-up, documentation, intellectual property rights (IPR), and marketing strategies to evaluate pharmaceutical product development and commercialization. Analyze the roles of research and development (R&D) management, human resource development, industrial relations, and ethical practices in achieving sustainable and compliant pharmaceutical operations.

about: A study of physicochemical and biopharmaceutical factors involved in the design of novel drug delivery systems like mucosal, particulate systems for systemic delivery of bioactive molecules. title: Retrosynthetic Analysis
about: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course. Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug molecules with appropriate justification.
topics: Introduction & basic concepts of retrosynthetic analysis
One Group and Two Group C-C Disconnections
Two Group C-C Disconnections: 1,3-, 1,5-, 1,2- 1,4-, and 1,6 difunctionalized compounds
Buffer lectures, quizzes, discussion for specific topics, etc.

title: Pharmaceutical Applications of Polymers and Biopolymers
about: This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in contact with biological systems. Topics include molecular interactions between bioand synthetic molecules and surfaces; design, synthesis, and processing approaches for materials that control cell functions; and application of state-of-the-art materials science to problems in tissue engineering, drug delivery, vaccines, and cell-guiding surfaces. This course covers the fundamental concepts (physical chemistry, chemistry, and materials physics, and biology) behind the design at a molecular scale of synthetic materials with biological functions.
topics: Classes of Materials Used in Medicine
Key Concepts in the Use of Biomaterials in Surgery and Medical Devices
Host Reaction to Biomaterials and Their Evaluation
Applications of Biomaterials in Functional Tissue Engineering

title: Classical Mechanics
about: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames. To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity.  Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.  Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.  Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.  Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects.
topics: Vector Algebra: Basic Operations, Differential Operators (Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian) in curvilinear coordinate systems, Multivariable Calculus (total derivatives and chain rule)
Newtonian mechanics for a particle/system of particles: Conservation principles, etc.
Constrained Motions: Classification of constraints. Degree of freedom (DOF), generalized coordinates.
Systematic methods to eliminate/bypass constraints, Principle of virtual work, d’Alembert’s principle (may shock you at first and certainly test your patience!), Euler- Lagrange’s (E-L) equation
Setting up the problem through Lagrangian approach: Reduction of two-body problem to an equivalent one-body problem.
Two first integrals of motion, classification of orbits based on bounded/unbounded motion, stability criteria, closure property, etc.
Orbits under inverse-square law of force, any deviation from inverse square law? Qualitative understanding of precession of orbits via phenomenological model.
Principle of least action : Fermat’s principle in optics, Geodesics for material bodies, Material bodies in conservative force fields (Brachistochrone, Tautochrone, etc.)
Derivation of the Euler– Lagrange Equations from Hamilton’s principle
Derivation of conserved quantities from the symmetries of the Lagrangian
Construction of the Hamiltonian from Lagrangian (the Lagrangian's twin sibling!) through duality transformation.
Four basic CTs and the corresponding generating functions (GF)
Poisson bracket and other canonical invariants (where you start sensing quantum mechanics lurking in the background!)
Independent Coordinates, Orthogonal Transformations, Formal properties of transformation matrix
Euler Angles, Finite and Infinitesimal Rotations
Rate of Change of a vector, Coriolis Effects (hard to avoid when you're sitting in a lecture room on the rotating Earth!)
