title: STATISTICAL MECHANICS
about: This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions. ❖ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics. ❖ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of thermodynamic systems ❖ Learn key methods of ensemble theory ❖ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems.

Thermodynamics and Kinetic Description.(Number of lectures: 7)

thermodynamics. Empirical temperature scales. Dilute gases and ideal gas temperature. Thermometry. Equation of state. Internal Energy. How to understand the concept of temperature in classical thermodynamics?

2 Introduction to heat, work, and internal energy. First law of thermodynamics. Applications of the first law of Thermodynamics. If energy conservation is known in mechanics, what is the need for the first law of thermodynamics? What is heat?
3 Kinetic theory of dilute gases. Pressure, temperature, and internal energy.
4 Description of dynamics in Phase space, Mu-space, and distribution function. Maxwell’s velocity distribution
5 Carnot’s engine, The Second Law of Thermodynamics, Entropy, and Clausius’s inequality. What is the limitation of the first law?

title: Particle Physics
about: (Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the course.) What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the Universe? What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural hierarchy we see at different levels? What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above questions? Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the answers we know? Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. Answers to questions 1 and 2 have been the content of the latter half of your Nuclear and Particle Physics course. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure. Symmetry transformations can be continuous or discrete. Discrete symmetries are essentially invariances under a discrete transformation and will be the subject of module-4. Their examples are parity (P) (inversion about origin, i.e., changing x,y,z to -x,-y,-z), time reversal (T) (changing t to -t), and charge conjugation (C) (changing particles to antiparticles and vice versa). Naively, Physics was expected to be invariant under each of these discrete transformations separately. However, it turns out that individually, each of them is violated. In fact, the so-called CPT theorem states that any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with a Hermitian Hamiltonian must be invariant under the combined transformation of Charge conjugation (C), Parity (P), and Time reversal (T). It turns out that the weak interactions violate all three (C, P, and T) and also the combination CP. However, the combined CPT transformation is so far known to be an exact symmetry and any violation of CPT would signal a fundamental trouble either in quantum mechanics or relativity or local interactions. The Story of the separate violations of C, P, and T is intricately tied to the story of weak interaction and will be covered in module 5. 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Module-6 would be the last module of the course and will answer question number 4 in the affirmative and offer a convincing discourse on the same. Until the advent of Particle Physics in the 20th century, symmetries and conservation laws largely served a utilitarian purpose of bookkeeping. Conservation laws offer our first shot at dynamics without having to confront the dynamics head-on. Just look at the stuff before and after a dynamical event, and if conservation laws are applicable, we can pull out the unknown energy or momentum by a straightforward bookkeeping of conserved quantum numbers. However, during the latter half of the 20th century, we learnt that the symmetries aren’t just utilitarian. They are the rhyme and the reason behind why things are the way they are. What do you need to build the Universe from scratch? The bricks (fundamental particles), the cement (glue to bind them to form bound states), and a blueprint (the Lagrangian). All of these and much more are a consequence of some symmetry principles which can be broadly divided into two categories -- spacetime symmetries (Lorentz or, strictly speaking, Poincaré symmetries), and internal or local gauge symmetries. So the question of kinematics, or why the fundamental particles of different mass and spin exist at all, is answered by the spacetime symmetries. Particles of different mass and spin exist as representations of Poincare group. On the other hand, the question of the existence of three different fundamental interactions (excluding gravity for the moment) is answered by the "internal" local gauge symmetries. They are "internal" in the sense that they operate in an abstract internal space different from the "external" spacetime. All the fundamental interactions are explained within the overarching theme of gauge theories. If you think the question is an oxymoron and with a blatant misuse of adjectives, please bear with me until the mist clears. We now have the basic building blocks (particles) and the glue (interactions) which bind them in place as a consequence of spacetime (Poincaré) and internal (Gauge) symmetries. But what is the origin of the mass of the particles? It turns out that you cannot just put a mass term in your fundamental Lagrangian by hand and get on with the business. The question of mass is intricately tied to the question of Lorentz invariance and gauge invariance, and will be covered in the latter half of module 6. In a jigsaw puzzle, each piece is constrained by the shape of the neighbouring pieces. We cannot accommodate mass without fundamentally tweaking the particle content and introducing a "subtle breaking" of the gauge symmetries. There are three different ways in which a symmetry can be broken: explicit, spontaneous, and anomalous (beyond the scope of the course). It turns out that putting a mass term by hand explicitly breaks the local gauge symmetry, and that is nothing short of a sacrilege in particle physics. We can nevertheless break it through the "back door", that is, break it spontaneously! Our Lagrangian, equations of motion, commutation relations, and Feynman rules all respect gauge symmetry, and yet, the choice of a ground state violates the symmetry. Spontaneous symmetry breaking may appear mysterious, but it is rather common. The most famous example is that of a ferromagnet. Its Hamiltonian is invariant under rotational symmetry. This is why, above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature, thanks to thermal agitation, all the spin dipoles are randomly oriented and hence the net magnetization averages out to zero. However, below the Curie temperature, all dipoles spontaneously align in a specific direction, giving non-zero net magnetization. The Hamiltonian is still rotationally invariant, and yet magnetic dipoles select a specific direction and align. It turns out that to realize such spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics, we need to add a spin-0 field and its accompanying dynamics. How exactly the machinery of the Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking end up endowing fundamental particles with mass cannot be elaborated here. It is said that the proof of the pudding is in eating. We hope to get this far and discuss these issues. 3 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division We started with bright blue skies and end with dark clouds. I wish I could end this preface on a positive note. However, truth be told, all of our knowledge about fundamental particles and their interactions is like a small lamp in a largely dark room. I am collecting here a laundry list of questions about which we have only speculations to offer without any hint of empirical verification. Dark matter and dark energy: All of our understanding of the Universe encoded in the standard model of physics accounts for merely 5% of the observed Universe. The remaining 95 % consists of dark matter (27%) and dark energy (68%). The word here represents not only our ignorance about their origin and nature, but also that neither of these two forms of energy in the universe interacts directly with the known particles via known interactions. - except through gravity. Neutrinos are massive and mixed: Neutrinos are massless within the standard model, but they are now known to have tiny non-zero masses, and the three species of neutrinos are also known to mix among themselves. To explain neutrino masses and mixing, we need to extend the standard model by introducing new particles and/or new interactions. Matter-antimatter asymmetry: Although the laws of physics are largely symmetric under the particle-antiparticle exchange, the observed universe is grossly asymmetric. Theories that explain this asymmetry go by the name of baryogenesis (generating an excess of baryons over anti-baryons). There are scores of models, but none that have been empirically verified. The Flavour Problem: We introduced the Higgs boson to explain the masses of fundamental particles, but the introduction of the entire Higgs sector is ad-hoc and poses more problems than it claims to solve. Why are there only three generations of quarks and leptons? Why is there a clear hierarchy of masses across generations? Why do masses take the value they take? The Standard Model cannot answer any of these questions. Gravity is excluded: Notice that we have kept gravity out of the scheme of things. That is because gravity is very different from other forces in that we do not yet have a consistent and complete quantum theory of gravity that works at all energy scales. There are a few more fundamental problems, but they are beyond the scope of this handout. The above description conveys the scope and objective in great detail.

title: SOFT CONDENSED MATTER PHYSICS
about: Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations. They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant. In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter. What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter? Develop familiarity with the basics of soft condensed matter. To develop an understanding about the forces and order of thermal fluctuations in soft matter. Why some part of matter is classified as soft matter?

title: Group Theory and Applications
about: This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions. Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras.
topics: Introduction of the course in view of its necessity in the context of fundamental physics; the course structure will be briefed
—L3: Importance of symmetry in nature and in natural law, groups as the language of symmetry, definition and introduction.

—L7: Subgroups, cosets, invariant and normal subgroups, quotient groups and product groups, Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms. L8—L12: Group representation: unitary representation, reducible and irreducible representation, direct sum and tensor products, character table, Schur’s lemmas.

—L17: Lie groups, infinitesimal transformation, Jacobi identity, structure constants, killing forms, subalgebras; Real and Complex Lie algebra, Irreducible representations of Lie groups and Lie algebras; Adjoint Representations.

—L20: Rotations and Angular Momentum, SO(3) and SU(2), Infinitesimal rotations and generators, covering groups, applications, introduction to Spinor representations, Clifford algebra, Dirac matrices, Majorana and Weyl fermions, Representations of SU(3), Pauli vs Gell-Mann matrices
—L24: Relativistic symmetries, Lorentz and Poincaré groups, introduction to particle representations, Casimir operators.

—L38: Introduction to Cartan-Weyl basis, Classification of simple Lie algebras, Roots and weights, Dynkin diagrams, SU(3) representations revisited, Eightfold way, Isospin, Meson and Baryon masses, symmetry breaking, color, introduction to Abelian and Non-Abelian gauge groups

title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices
about: This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed. The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of the basic phenomenon of the semiconductor devices. The main content of the course is having theoretical description of these devices which is an essential requirement in order to understand the operational details of any device.

title: Classical and Quantum Waves
about: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling. Understand oscillatory motion: Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes, and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling waves, and energy transport Analyze wave behavior and propagation: Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division energy quantization in simple systems Apply quantum tunneling to real-world technology: Calculate transmission coefficients for barrier tunneling and connect this phenomenon to practical applications such as scanning tunneling microscopy Develop the ability to analyze and understand oscillatory mechanical systems that are coupled Ability to solve the wave equation for certain boundary conditions To understand Interference and diffraction phenomena To describe wave-particle duality and the photon concept, derive the de Broglie wavelength for matter waves, and articulate the physical meaning of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle Solve the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a one-dimensional box, interpret the resulting wavefunctions, and calculate the quantized energy levels of the system Calculate the transmission coefficient for a particle tunneling through a potential barrier, and explain how this phenomenon underlies the operation of a scanning tunneling microscope
topics: Effect of Viscous Damping, Decay of Free Vibrations, Quality Parameter, Light Damping, Critical Damping, Heavy Damping

title: Introduction to Classical and Quantum Waves
about: Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves, introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications; Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers. This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines. Explain the principles of simple harmonic motion and analyze damped and forced oscillations, resonance, and the superposition of oscillatory motion as the foundation of wave phenomena. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Describe the behavior of classical waves, including wave propagation, wave equations, energy transport, sound waves, and the formation of standing waves in one-dimensional systems. Explain the wave nature of light through interference and diffraction and discuss the experimental observations that established the quantum nature of light, including the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. Describe the concept of matter waves by explaining wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the extension of wave concepts from light to material particles. Interpret the physical meaning of quantum wave functions in one dimension and explain their role in describing quantum systems, including an introductory understanding of multi-electron atoms through Pauli's exclusion principle and the principles of X-rays and lasers.

title: Advanced Operations Management
about: Types of Manufacturing, Manufacturing, maintenance, quality and service operations management concepts. Manufacturing Management measures, Factory/plant performance, Operations Improvement framework. Maintenance management, optimising maintenance costs; Improving asset lifecycle; Preventive maintenance; Total productive maintenance (TPM); Quality management - practices and processes; Total quality management (TQM); Service Operations Management definition; Customer loyalty and satisfaction. This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and maintenance management as practised on the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed. This will help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain. This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various quality management tools and techniques used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and services are produced. This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design, service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed.
topics: Course introduction. Definition and scope of operations management. Role of operations management in organisations. Functions and challenges of operations management. Types of manufacturing (job, batch, mass, continuous). Product-process matrix: linking volume- variety with process choice. Breakeven Analysis.

Numerical: takt time and throughput calculation for a given demand/production scenario. Capacity utilisation and efficiency measures. The bathtub curve and product failure behaviour; predicting failures with condition monitoring; understanding the P-F interval and the P-F curve; selecting a maintenance strategy based on machine asset type; functional blocks of digital maintenance; and sustainability aspects.

Measuring failures and KPIs: failure rate, MTTF, MTBF, MTTR, downtime, availability, maintainability. Maintenance trade-offs: preventive cost vs. breakdown cost, optimal maintenance interval. Preventive Maintenance (PM) modelling. Hands-on exercise for designing PM schedules.

This course will give students a broad overview of the fundamental theories regarding various logistics functions and their overall management. With this course, students will be able to approach logistics management with a holistic view and understand, analyse, and coordinate various functions within a coherent supply chain framework. This will help students understand the various components of procurement – sourcing, contracting, supplier management, qualification management, purchasing of direct and indirect materials, spend analysis, and its integration with other management systems/applications. This will help explore the importance of inventory management, the key components involved, and the best practices that businesses can implement to improve their inventory management processes.
topics: Course introduction. Introduction to logistics: definition, scope, objectives, components, and importance of logistics. Types of logistics (procurement, production, distribution, reverse, after-sales, global, domestic). Role of logistics in manufacturing and the economy. Difference between logistics and supply chain management. Supply chain relationships. Case study.

Mathematical formulation of transportation and distribution models. Quantitative techniques to obtain an initial basic feasible solution for balanced and unbalanced transportation problems. Northwest Corner Method (NWCM). Least Cost Method. Hands-on numerical examples.

Quantitative Techniques to determine optimal movement of goods between plants, warehouses, and customers. Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM) for obtaining high-quality initial solutions. Comparison of

different initial solution methods and their efficiencies. Optimal transportation plans. MODI method. Degeneracy. Solving maximisation transportation problems. Spreadsheet implementation. Interpreting results for managerial decision-making.
Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP). Vehicle Routing Problems (VRP). Distribution routing strategies. Logistics routing applications. Case studies and optimisation exercises.

Transportation network planning. Integration of transportation with distribution planning. Carrier selection. Transportation performance measures. Strategic transportation decisions and industry applications.

Introduction to inventory management and its role in supply chains. Objectives and functions of inventory. Types and classifications of inventory (raw materials, WIP, finished goods, MRO). Inventory transactions, including receipts, issues, transfers, returns, adjustments, and stock verification. Inventory cost components include ordering, holding, shortage, and purchasing costs. Hands- on exercises on inventory classification and inventory transaction scenarios with practical numerical examples.

Continuous demand, instantaneous replenishment model. Inventory replenishment concepts and assumptions of the EOQ model. Development and mathematical derivation of the EOQ model. Analysis of total inventory cost, reorder point, and inventory cycle. Sensitivity analysis and managerial interpretation of EOQ. Step-by-step solution of a variety of numerical problems and hands-on implementation.
Economic Production Quantity (EPQ) model and its applications. Quantity

title: Management Accounting
about: Success in any organization—from the smallest corner store to the largest multinational corporation—requires the use of cost accounting concepts and practices. Cost accounting provides key data to managers for planning and controlling, as well as costing products, services, even customers. Cost accounting is one of very important managerial tool for business strategy and implementation. This course focuses on how cost accounting helps managers make better decisions, as cost accountants are increasingly becoming integral members of their company’s decision-making teams. This course will equip students with the knowledge and analytical skills required to apply management accounting tools and techniques for planning, decision making, cost control, and performance evaluation in organizations.

title: Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology
about: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered. The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.
topics: Course introduction, what is nanoscience and nanotechnology? Difference between micro and nano, classification of nanostructured materials, unique properties of nanomaterials: structural, electronic, magnetic, optical, mechanical.
Bottom-up: physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), sol- gel, spray conversion, wet chemical synthesis, self- assembly
Top-Down: Mechanical alloying, equal channel angular pressing, high-pressure torsion (HPT), accumulative roll bonding (ARB), Nanolithography
Basics of quantum physics, wave mechanics, Schrödinger wave equation, concepts of quantum well, wire and dots, tunneling, applications of quantum mechanics in nanotechnology.
Synthesis, properties, and applications of carbon nanostructures: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, nanodiamonds, and diamond-like carbon (DLC).
Applications of nanotechnology in electronics: Basics of semiconductor devices, MOSFETs, FinFETs
Application of nanotechnology in medical devices: Basics of bio- electronic devices, nanosensors, molecular imaging, targeted drug delivery applications.
Application of nanotechnology in MEMS: Basics of MEMS/NEMS, fabrication techniques, working principles of accelerometers, and actuators.
Basics of fuel cells and batteries, nanotechnology applications in fuel cells, energy storage devices.
Basics of catalysis, synthesis of metal and oxide active phases, nanoreactors.
Nanofluids Synthesis, characterization and applications relevant to heat transfer. State of the art and future research directions.
Large scale manufacture and technological issues

title: Fundamentals of Solid-State Physics
about: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology. This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses. Describe crystal structures, Bravais lattices, crystal systems, common crystal structures, and Miller indices, and explain their significance in determining the physical properties of crystalline solids. Apply the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to explain wave-particle duality, quantized energy levels, and the origin of electronic states in solids. Differentiate between Maxwell–Boltzmann, Bose–Einstein, and Fermi–Dirac statistics, and explain the statistical behavior of electrons and other particles in solids. Explain electrical conduction in solids using the Drude model and band theory, and relate density of states and effective mass to the electronic properties of materials. Analyze the electrical properties of intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors and explain carrier transport through drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Explain the thermal and magnetic properties of solids in terms of lattice vibrations, phonons, heat capacity, and magnetic ordering. Explain the optical properties of semiconductors and relate them to the operation of optoelectronic devices, including LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and semiconductor sensors.

§ Wave equation, Schrödinger equation, Superposition, Expectation values § Solution of Schrödinger equation: Particle in a box, Finite potential well, tunneling

Electrons in Solids and Band Theory

§ Classical free electron model; Electrical conduction: Drift velocity, mobility, conductivity; Need for quantum description § Band theory: Valence and Conduction bands, Kronig-Penney model § Classification of solids: Metals, Semiconductors, and Insulators § Conceptual introduction of density of states, Idea of effective mass

§ Intrinsic semiconductors: Electron-hole pairs, carrier density, temperature effect § Extrinsic semiconductors: Donor impurities (n-type) and Acceptor impurities (p-type) § Carrier transport: Drift, diffusion; Hall effect
§ Thermal properties: Lattice vibrations § Magnetic properties: Diamagnetism, Paramagnetism, and Ferromagnetism
§ Optical properties and applications: Photoconductivity, Solar cells, Photodetectors, LEDs

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
about: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
about: Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science concepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, design, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in parallel with the software development life cycle. This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions Understand and apply fundamental software engineering principles throughout the software development life cycle. Identify, formulate, and solve complex software engineering problems using appropriate engineering, scientific, and mathematical principles. Elicit, specify, and analyze software requirements for real-world systems. Design structured, modular, and maintainable software systems. Develop, test, and maintain software using modern tools and best practices. 1 Function effectively as a member or leader of a diverse team, demonstrating collaboration and project management skills. Plan and manage software projects, including task estimation, scheduling, and risk analysis. Demonstrate awareness of ethical, legal, and societal issues in software engineering.

title: Social Conduct 1
about: Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity & Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety. This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior and building awareness against substance abuse. At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community.
